INDIANAPOLIS, Nov. 1.-THE DEM
ocratic landslide struck Indiana. Not
only was Woodrow Wilson carried by
it's force with Governor Thomas K
Marshall. but the entire state ticket
the legislature and the congressional
delegation is Democratic. Edward
Dean Crumpacker, who for years has
represented the Tenth district, and who
was the only Republican representative
in congress from the state at the last
congress. has been defeated, according
to latest returns from the northern part
of the state.


The congressman elected are: First
district, Charles F. Lied; Second dis
trict. William A. Cullop; Third dis
trict, William E. Cox; Fourth district,
Lincoln Diedon; Fifth district Ralph
w. Moss; Sixth district, Finley Fl.
Gray; Seventh district Charles A.
Korbly; Eighth district, John A. M.
Adair; Ninth district, Martin A. Nor
rison; Tenth district, John Peterson;
Eleventh district, George w. Rauch;
Twelfth district, Cyrus Cline; Thir-
teenth district. Henry A. Barnhart.

resumed the stand today to tell the
story of her relations with Jack John
son. the colored heavyweight champion
pugilist of the world. to the Federal
grand jury, Upon her evidence. the
government expects to secure an indict-
ment against the black champion for
alleged violations of the Mann act

the hysterical attack which followed
two hours questioning on the stand
yesterday when she defied the jurors
and prosecutor All traces of bravado
had disappeared today. While it was
said the government did not expect to
indict Johnson for bringing the Cam
eron girl to Chicago, her testimony
with that of other witnesses, was ex-
pected to show he had brought other
women to Chicago from other states.

last night denouncing Johnson and
urging the revocation of his license.

The great deeps were conquered with diving
bell long ago, and more recently with the subma-
rines. The aeroplane has assumed dominion of the
skies, and is being brought more and more to per-
fecton. After both poles had been discovered there
seemed to be nothing this terrestrial ball left that
was worthy Of real adventurers and discoveries.


Then the director of the observatory on Mt
Vesuvius bethought him that nobody had ever yet
sounded the depths of volcano and come out alive
That early philosopher, Empedocles, projected him
self into the suphurous innards of Mt. Etna but he
failed to return with any scientific data, and one
shoe, cast up with the scoriae and ashes, was the
only memorial of his fate.


The equipment, we'll as the courage of the
twentieth century was drawn upon by the Vesuvius
professor for his hazardous exploration. He took
along with him moving picture operator who was
to bring back indubitable films as an evidence of
good faith. They walked about on the floor of the
crater, photographed the vapors, and other phe-
nomena, and reached the outside worlu safely again
While they hardly penetrated the entire crust of the
earth, they sensiby narrowed the one remaining
field of exploration, and by now are busy throwing
the pictures the screen. Much valuable data has
also been brought forward. In very truth the dar-
ing souls of the future who would win the laurels
of the pioneer will find, whether they direct their
gaze to earth, sea- or sky that they were born too
late.

Municipal ownership has received a big
boost in western Iowa because of the
successful year which the Council Bluffs
city water works has just closed. The
annual report, just issued, shows that in
addition to paying off the interest on the
investment. spending $4,000 in better
ments and repairs. the city has cleared
approximately $4,000, which sum will be
set aside to assist i'm paying the bonds
when they fall due. Enemies of mu-
nicipal ownership have been converted.
The Council Bluffs water plant was
built nearly thirty years ago. Since then
its owners have received regular dividends
of about IL per cent and more, while
practically nothing has been expended for
betterments and repairs. In fact. much
of the antiauated machinery which was
installed when the plant was constructed
was still in use when the city took over
the system. The fight for possession of
the water works was waged for eight
wears The company exhausted every
legal technicality to maintain its hold
on the profitable business. but advocates
of city ownership fought the battle to
a successful finish and in July, 1911, the
system was turned over to the city.
Council Bluffs issued longtime bonds,
which were sold, and the money received
from the sale was paid over TO the water
company and the city took the plant.
Simply the city's credit was used. And
the first years profits are SO remarkable
that the citizens see In the near future
that they will have sufficient cash with
which to pay Of all Indebtedness. thus
securing ownership of the entire system
without the expenditure of single cent
New settling basins have been construct
ed and big storage basins are being built
Many miles of new pipes have been laid
and repairs and betterments are being
made in every department of the system
And alt without "a cents increase in rate
or charge to the citizens.

After having travelled four days on


snowshoes across the continental divide,


Mrs. Walter Mullins, sixteen years old.
arrived in Steamboat Springs, recently,


nearly dead from exhaustion and the ef-


fects of the suns reflection from the snow


which blistered her face, neck and arms


until they were covered with bleeding


sores. She fell exhausted when she got
into the town, having made the trip to


reach the bedside of her sister. Miss Rose


Morgan, who Is seriously i'll.


Men accustomed to snowshoes and


mountain travel shrink from the trip


across Buffalo pass in winter. The snow


lay sixteen to fifty feet deep along the


path of Mrs. Mullins journey. but she


pushed forward with the dauntlessness of


an Arctic explorer.


Mrs. Mullins is typical mountain girl


She lived on her fathers ranch at May


bell until she eloped in July, 1910. with
Mullins, who was employed as a cow
puncher. She was then only fourteen
years old.


Mullins and the girl fled across the
mountains with the girls father in pur-
suit They req ched Rock Springs, Wyo.,
in the lead, but the father put the sher-
iff on their track and they were arrest
ed, but 1t was evident that the girl want
ed to marry him and the father relented.
Mrs. Mullins and her husband had been
living across the divide. When word
reached her that her sister was not ex-
pected to live she buckled on her snow


shoes and, in spite of the desolate coun-
try, where snowstorms and billiards. are
frequent and deadly, set out on the four
day journey, carrying with her enough
food for the trip.

DUBLIN. June q, 1912.


mass meeting Of Irish suffra gists was
held this week In the ancient concert
rooms, Dublin. The meeting was unique
in that it was the first time that Irish
women from the north, east, south and
west-women of all shades OF political
opinion, suffragists militant and non mill
tant-were gathered together unitedly to
demand a government amendment In the
home rule bill enfranchising rrishwomen

nants. the orange and green of the
Franchise League and its branches; the
declarations: the dark blue and gold Of the
daughters Of Erin. while all round the
hall. the second largest in Dublin, were
ranged shields bearing the names of the
various centers which had sent delegates
The platform was occupied exclusively by
women, and all the speakers were wom-
en-town councillors, graduates from the
two Irish universities, poor law guar
dams, woman doctors, working women
artists. actresses. teachers. nurses-pre-
sided over by Miss Hayton the lady sena-
tor of the national university


The societies represented were the
Irishwomens Franchise League. the
Irishwomen's Reform League, the Irish
women's Suffrage Society. Belfast, the
Munster Women's Franchise League the
Irish League for Women Suffrage, Lon
don: Waterford. Lisburn, Newry, War
renpoint, Birr. Armagh. Limerick, Derry
and Wexford suffrage societies: the
Irshwomens Workers Union. the Ladies'
Committee and the Irish Diapers Assist
ants Association.

read from the Rev. ]. o. Hanney, Nine.
Maude Come. Miss Malone. George Rus
sell. Miss O'ConnelI Hayes, DR.. Sophia
Bryant. Mrs. Dryhurst. James Connolly,
Miss Patricia Hoey and others. Cable
grams were received from Miss Vida
Goldstein. representing the Womens Po-
litfcal Association of Victoria and from
the woman suffragists OF America


The following resolution was adopted:


That. while expressing no opinion on
the general question of home rule, this
mass meeting Of delegates from the Irish
suffrage societies and other women's or
CARNATIONS. representing all shadse OF
political and religious opinion. profound
ly regrets the proposal to establish a new
constitution In Ireland on a purely male
franchise. and calls upon the government
to amend the home rule bill in commit
tee by adopting the local government
register, which includes women. as the

HENLEY ON THAMES. England
July 6-The Henley regatta, Englands 6
famous water carnival, today reached
the eliminating point in all the big
events and, for the first time since its
institution in 1889. received the pa
tronage of the king. His majesty. ac-
complained by the queen and Princess
Mary, came from London to Henley by
train.


On arriving King George and Queen
Mary embarked on the royal barge.
which was brilliantly emblazoned with
red and gold and manned by the kings
watermen in their liveries of centuries
ago. Their majesties then proceeded
down the course to the royal standard,
from which they watched the final
heats of the British aquatic champion
ships.


Good Weather for Occasion.


Beautiful weather today favored the
occasion, in marked contrast to the days
that preceded, and the scene on the
river was one Of unforgottable brilliance.
with gayly decorated houseboats. more
modest punts, skiffs and canoes lining
the course.


During the afternoon the royal party
proceeded the full length Of the course
and received most hearty welcome.


The barge used today was built by
King William III for Queen Mary in
1889. and is one Of the oldest vessels In
England. 1t was used for many years
to convey the English kings and queens
between their royal residences at Green
wich and Westminster.

courageously resumed with the same gun

Sourrieu, commander of the training ship

character ever recorded. For many years
these sudden cyclonic storms have swept
through the western country, where the
fiatness gives them tremendous sweep
without interruption. swoOping down upon
cities and towns and hamlets with practi-
cally no warning. sometimes cutting a
narrow swath. again laying waste the en-
tire settlement. The freaks of these hur-
ricanes are numerous and startling in
their eccentricity-buildings cut in half.
steeples lifted bodily from churches other
wise unharmed. roofs blown from their
original buildings to the tops of other
buildings far away. houses carried entire
from their foundations and set down with
little injury at distance. great struc-
lures torn into the smallest conceivable
fragments, trees uprooted and driven
through walls, human beings blown far
through the air and landed without hurt.

NEW YORK, June 3.-Trade authorities
say that IL costs more to live now than
ever before in the history Of the United
States. except perhaps during war times.
Prices were high a year ago, but today
they are claimed to be on the average
nearly 10 per cent higher.


Food products are the highest on rec
ord. Meat, eggs. butter. fish. potatoes.
coffee. tea, sugar, moiasses, rice. beans
and peas average 81 per cent higher;
wheat. corn. oats. barley, flour. ETC., 33
per cent higher.


Fruits are the only things good to eat
that have grown cheaper during the last
twelve months. but they are still higher
than in 1910. Leather products cost Il
per cent and chemicals and drugs 10 per
cent more than a year ago.


Textile goods, however. are tribe
cheaper.


The average increase in food products
is nearly 20 per cent. which means that
the housewife must pay So to I'LL a market
basket that cost her only So to fill in
June, 1911; in other words, 81 will buy
only fve-sixths as much as 1t did a year
ago. The biggest advances have been in
eat products-beef 20 per cent: hog
products, ~ per cent. and mutton over
- per cent. Dealers lay the increase to
last years poor hay crop and the gen.
eral high cost OF animal provender


Poor crops are also held responsible for
tearer breadstuffs.


Economists differ as to the reasons for
the general upward tendency of all COM
modities during. recent years. which has
been worldwide.

text:
A late dispatch announced that "the
deadly drinking cup has closed its career
IN Kentucky. the recently enacted statute
prohibiting its use having become opera
tive. The new law finds it's way
made plain by public sentiment, which
had already accomplished the object
in most of the cities. Railroads have
carried notices for several weeks pre-
pairing travellers for the change"


Thus Kentucky is added to the long
and growing list of states that have
abandoned the drinking cup. Sanitary
reform goes forward. The transition
from the germ-covered common drink
ing vessel to the individual cup has
been rapid and the world has not COM
pleteiy adjusted itself to the changed
conditions. The abolition of the dip
per that hung by the fountain or pump
and of the railway glass that was
handled and rehandled until its con-
dition was unsightly and dangerous
has been brought about so quickly that
not In all instances have satisfactory
substitutes been provided.


The bubbling fountain is playing its
part well. but the paper cup which
must be paid for sometimes dis
courages or postpones perhaps the
taking of a drink of water. Better a
little thirst. though. than tuberculosis.
typhoid. diphtheria or any of the thou
sand ills that Turk in the public cup.
headline: Kentucky Bans Public Cup.

PITTSBURG, Pa, Jan. 10.-Burglars
entered the residence OF Thomas p.
Jones, vice-president of the Pitts
burgh- Buffalo Coal Co. In the fashion
able district of Hardwood, a suburb,
and after chloroforming Mrs. Jones
and binding her with loose telephone
wires ransacked the house early today
and took $3.50 In cash, from beneath
the mattress of the bed.


The thieves secured napkin from
the dining room and saturated Il with
chloroform. They quietly made their
way to the second floor room where
the coal magnate's wife and 12-year-
old daughter Annabel were sleeping.
Mr.. Jones has been out OF town for
several days.


Mrs. Jones was awakened by two
men standing by her bed. She tried
to scream. but remembers nothing
more. The daughter stumbled over her
mother lying unconscious on the floor
this morning and aroused the rest OF
the household The police were noti-
fed and vigorous search Is being
made. II is thought the men were
frightened away before they completed
the search OF the house.

Frank Wrenn, his brother. William

of their lives yesterday afternoon before

Vigilant.


The two Wrenn boys live at 2505 l
street northwest, while young Brown
home is at 2141 E street. The boys, with
other companions. some time ago con-
structed a raft Of drift-wood, which they
had anchored at the government wharf.
Here they have been in the habit of
playing pirate or sailor, and have used
the raft as a platform from which to
make fancy dives while swimming in the
river.


Yesterday afternoon the three boys, with
three others about their age, were play
ing on the raft, when the moorings that
held it to the shore became unfastened.
The raft had drifted several feet from
the wharf before the boys noticed their
predicament Three of the boys promptly
sprang overheard and swan ashore.


Refuse to Desert Frank.


The two Wrenn boys and young Brown,
however, stayed. William Wrenn, who is
twelve years old, can swim. and SO can
Clifton Brown. But Frank Wrenn, who
is only ten, can't. and the two lads re-
fused to desert him.


The raft drifted out into the current and
down the river. with the boys calling for
help that failed to come. At the High
way bridge Frank Wrenn was crying,
and the older boys were trying to COM
fort him and at the same time keep up
their own courage by saying that some
one would soon come and take them off
the raft.


Then the Vigilant came along. The boys
were taken off the raft and the Vigilant
bore them safe to shore, while the frail
craft that had served them as plaything
and then had treacherously carried them
down the river f1oated on down the
stream.

Philadelphia. July 6.-The Aero Club. of

day, adopted resolution asking Congress
to pass laws establishing air routes and

probably take up the matter with other
members of the lower House for the
club. A committee from the Aero Club

At the Olympic games at Stockholm
there was used novel electric
method for timing the runners In some
OF the races, SO as to get the exact
time made by the winner, and also to
decide who crossed the line first. even
when the difference was very small
The starter gave the signal by firing
a pistol and this was connected by
electric wires with two stop watches
and these commenced to run for TAX.
ing the time. The start and finish
were at the same point, and across the
track light string was stretched be.
tween poles and the string was also
connected with the stop watches for
stopping them. The first conner broke
the string when crossing the line SO
that the watches were stopped and the
exact time between start and finish
could be seen. Breaking the string
also served to work an electric device
for the shutter Of camera which was
mounted just on the finish line and
above the judges stand. SO that the
photographer had an image Of the win.
ner when crossing the finish line.
This method Is very useful In settling
all disputes,--La Nature, Paris.

Mneola, Long Island. Dec. 2.-Arguins

Nassau term OF the Supreme Court this
morning, Miss Helen l.. Piguet not only
convinced the court and jury that she
was competent TO care for her estate. but
also that she was able to dispense with a
lawyer.


The action to have her declared ncom-
petent was brought by her sister. Lydia
s Piguet. who said I'm her complaint that
her sister was forty years old, unmar-
rled. and a well-to-do resident OF Wood
bury Long Island.


The complainant says her sister has
been OF unsound mind since 1858 and that
she was an inmate Of the State Hospital
for one year. but was discharged at the
end Of that time as improved. The COM
plainant also declares that her sister was
constantly talking religion, insisting her
religious blessings had been taken from
her by her enemies.


Justice Kelly asked the alleged incom-
petent what she wanted to do with her
money, and she replied that she wanted
10 give It to the poor. She also gave her
ideas Of religion.


The lawyer for the complainant told
Justice Kelly the reason she was incom-
petent was that she wanted to give her
money to the poor and did not dress In
the style OF the day but insisted in wear
ing old fashioned clothing. The court
rather tartly replied that lots OF people
were at large who did that. The jury de-
clafed the woman perfectly competent to
manage her affairs.

Two hundred fifty of the Central
City's enthusiastic boomers. headed by
Mayor Moore. many beautiful women
and the Macon bugle corps, breezed
into the Terminal station today in
special. six cars long. They came to
boost Macon. All day they did what
they came for. incidentally, they we're
royalty entertained at the Elks club by
the Atlanta Ad Mems association, after
they had made one of the most spec
tacular parades Peachtree street has
seen this summer


The invasion of the Maconites was
the idea of E. H. Hyman, secretary of
the Central City Chamber of Commerce.
the Guy Who Put the Con in Macon,
With Mayor Moore, w. T Anderson,
of The Telegraph, r. w. Armstrong ana
the PAS other boosters, he boarded the
train at the Central City at o'clock
and started out in blaze of Macon
bunting that startled the countryside
all the way along. The boosters
stopped at GAINESVILLE, Griffin and For
syth and paraded the main streets of
those towns with the redoubtable grey
coated buglers at their head.


Met BY AID Men.


When they reached Atlanta they
found the Terminal station thronged
with Interested spectators, who cheered
the invaders almost as heartily as the
invaders cheered their native town as
they detrained and marched. two and
two. to the plaza, where the parade
formed


The Atlanta AID association had
score of autos awaiting them, decked
out with red and white pennants and
red and white umbrellas fiaring forth
the inscription welcome to Our City"


But the men from Macon were not
to be outdone. They piled the autos
full of their own placards. prominent
among which stood out the chivalric
boast, Macon, Atlanta's Only Rival"


Into the automobiles climbed the Wis
iting women, Mayor Moore and the
Guy Who Put the Con In Macon
The other invaders formed in double
file on either side and, far back of the
machines, the bugles and drums struck
up a crashing fanfare and the long
parade started across to Peachtree.


There will never be any doubt in
anybodys mind after this about the
enthusiastic loyalty of Maconeers to
Macon. Those boosters had been rid
ing through a pretty warm country on
a warm train since : o'clock in the
morning. Three times enroute they
had left the train to parade, through
Georgia villages and shout out their
lungs for their favorite town,


Sun Didn't Wilt Them.


When they swung marching into
Peachtree street the sun was scorch
ing and they had long tramp UP hill.
But every one of them was smiling and
still brim full of enthusiasm So that
they cheered the crowds that swarmed
the pavements and the doorways and
windows, and then cheered some more
for Macon for good measure.


In one of the automobiles rode Miss
Eugenia Anderson. daughter of Man
ager Anderson of The Telegraph. and
the mascot of Macon Engenia hadn't
had a thing to eat since 7 o'clock and
she is only six years old and had been
in all the marching. But all the way
up Peachtree she flung an American
flag and waved Macon pennant so
vigorously that the crowds in the street
cheered her. because she was pretty
enough to be mascot for Atlanta.


Off Peachtree street the parade
swung into Auburn avenue and up
North Pryor street to the Ell<s club.


At the Elks club the Atlanta AID men
had fixed up Dutch luncheon which
the hungry men from Macon welcomed
with a cheer almost as enthusiastic as
those they continually expended upon
their city


Shortly after noon the boosters
marched over to the capitol to pay
their respects to the governor and the
general assembly


Unfortunately, the senate and house
both had adjourned, but the governor
came out listened to a couple of tunes
by the bugle corps, made short speech,
had his picture taken with them on the
steps and invited them to come again.

West African ant hills are veritable
giants, frequently standing forty feet
high. These ant hills are shaped some
thing like a sugar loaf and are divided
inside into hundreds of tiny rooms. They
have, needless to say, myriads of in
habitants, and these are all busiy occu-
pied in various ways-forming tunnels,
making roads, gathering food and watch
ing over the eggs and youngsters. The
natives are afraid to touch these hills,
except from a distance with firearms
The ants often make their strongholds
round trees, and they are built very SOL
idly, with sides sometimes twenty inches
thick. The inside is hollow, and at the
top there is a sort Of attic. The royal
CELL" where the queen ant lives, is al
ways found on the ground floor. This
good lady is a prisoner, but is carefully
fed by her busy subjects. the eggs she
lays being Immediately carried away and
deposited in rooms set apart for the
purpose.

new international balloon record for dis
lance has been made in the contest for
the Gordon Bennett cup, begun here Sun
day, by the French balloon Picardie,
which landed near Moscow, Russia, after
travelling 1854 miles. The old record,
made by Alan r. Hawley of the United
States, was LIZ miles.


While a French balloon had broken
the distance record, all chances of the
United States winning the contest had
not been wiped out, for one American
balloon, Uncle Sam, was still aloft so
far as known at noon. The unofficial
American entry, Dusseldorf II, was also
in the air


Twelve balloons had come down, ac-
cording to advices received by officials
here. This left seven official and unof-
fetal entries in the air.

NEW YORK. Dec "A heavy snow
storm, driven by high winds, is raging
along the Atlantic coast from Maine to
the Carolinas today. Although it ex-
tended we'll inland, the storm is most
severe along the coast, where it inter-
fered with shipping and delayed traffic
to a great extent in the cities in its
path. Reports of vessels ashore at
Barnegat and Sandy Hook reached here
early in the day.

Virginia capes north of Hatteras and
was moving northward.


In New York the snow was eight
inches deep. The snowfall throughout
the New England states was not heavy.
but the weather bureau predicted a
heavier fall before night in Maine and
New Hampshire.

inches during the night, while Chi
cago and indianapolis escaped without

W. Va. The snow that New Workers.
found bianketed upon the city when

ly handicapped surface and elevated
lines

DAYTON, OHIO, May 30.-Wilbur

heavier than air flying machine sue
cumbed to typhoid fever, and after

The end came after one of the most
remarkable struggles against the dis

For more than 36 hours Wright's tenn

105 degrees, while his respiration was

140. Stimulants were resorted to and.
for the last three days had been used

lants


Wonderful Vitality Shown.

Reuchlin Wright, younger brothers. Dr..
Conklin was in attendance when the
end came


Wilbur Wright's illness began a little
more than three weeks ago. He grew
rapidly worse and his condition be-
came critical within week after he
had been attacked by the malady


Orville Wright, brother of the in
ventor who was in Washington taking
up with government officials some mat
tiers in connection with the govern
ment's use of the Wright machines. was
summoned home. Shortly after he ar
rived cablegrams were sent to foreign
countries which the inventor had ex-
pected soon to visit, saving that it
would be impossible to make the trip
for some days. Then for the first time
it was known that Wilbur's condition
was such al to give grave alarm.


Wright rallied after the first sinking
spell and his wonderful vitality made
the physicians hope that he might re-
cover He aroused himself sufficiently
ito say that he would get well, and then
he srimly battled against death, fight
ing desperately against disease.


Made Game Fight For Life


A second sinking spell occurred, and
three days ago Dr. Conklin announced
that there was no hope. Wright sank
into state Of coma. He rallied slight
~, and though his fever was very high,
there seemed a slight chance that he
might recover The fight he made
caused the physician yesterday to issue
a hopeful statement.


Il do not know what the outcome wifi
be, he said Wright has remarkable
vitality and he is putting up gallant
fight. He may live l can not tell"


Wrights condition again took a turn
for the worse about midnight. He sank
into Inconsistencies and during the
last few hours was kept alive only
through stimulants.


Early today it was seen that the end
was not far off and the entire family
was summoned. All were in the room
when the aviator passed away


The aviators condition sank lower
and lower as the morning hours sped
by Shortly after o'clock it was
thought he was dying. His heart ac-
ton became very low The stimulants
eere again used and his heart respond
ed slightly. The final sinking spell be-
gan about 3 o'clock. He died peace
fully.

Orville Wright, the brother who has

sister Katherine. who helped the broth
ers when they We're struggling with
their invention and who shared their
triumpha European trip and their
home coming after the success of their
machines had been demonstrated,
though overcome herself. strove to
comfort Orvile.


Wrights mother is dead and his sis

Old Jack Frost is q festive fellow
He paints the Landscape brown and yellow.
On starry nights, when the air is still,
With silver mallet and crystal drill
He softly opens the chestnut burs
And lightly sprinkles a dusty furze
Over the haystacks the roofs, and walls
The cleaning pumpkins. like golden balls.
Across the meadows where moon-sprites sail
He silently spins spangled VEIL
While grooming cTickets in hedge and bower
Chip to the moon and the dying hour
Then on the hills and along the lanes,
Where the drowsy herd roams and complains
And the whippoor-will calls through the night,
In the dreamy moments crisp and bright.
Old Jack Frost slips with bewitching ease
And sTills his paint-pot over the trees
That glitter rays Of dazzling gems
In precious brooches and diadems.
Through the summer scenes and autumn haze
Where the quaint procession calmly strays
Far over the fields and through the woods,
Bedecked in russell and crimson hoods
That glisten and glow among the green,
While visions. trail to and fro between
The magic wickets and mystic bars
Where elves seem catching the falling stars
All flashing and fading in the light,
Through ulstling curtains, serene and bright,
As the passing days grow short and chill
And hush the rapture Of brook and rill,
Old Jack Frost roams with q spnghtly tread
Amid old trails where the flowers are dead.
Clipping the leaves with enchanted shears
And filling the eyes Of Time with tears.


GEORGE SANDS JOHNSON.

Boy Scouts in regulation uniform, some
of them bringing their little sisters and
some their parents. swarmed about the
entrance of the Cosmos Theater this
morning long before IL O'clock the time
for the benefit performance given for the
Ditrict Boy Scouts through the courtesy
of the mana cement.


The Boy Scout was "u" every minute
Of the performance Everything was done
to convince him that it was his per-
Torrance. When he entered the gates
a pretty miss in uniform showed him to a
seat, while A. ]. Brylawski, manager Of
the theater, halted him just long enough
to pin tiny American flag on his coat
No one was permitted to enter the thea
ter unless he could show an American
flag.


Reels showing the life of the real, live
Boy Scout were shown, and a short
vaudeville performance was given. The
theater resounded with cheers and vigor-
Gus hand-clapping of the boys.


Edwin Keller, the Mississippi whistler,
delighted the boys with numerous bird
calls. Every scout patrol has a bird call
by which it is known. and keller's whis-

amusing. Fred Grogan, the blind pianist,
and Miss Charlse. harpist, played, and the
Miranda quartet sang.


Then for the real fun, for the Boy
Scouts have their own ideas of their life
and it was correctly presented in the pic

showing delicate little moliycoddle who
fell into the Boy Scout ranks, and was
made a manly little fellow. The camp

NEW YORK, March 3o.-The United
States government has prepared papers
in suit to be filed for the dissolution Of
certain steamship companies engaged in
traffic between New York and the far
east by way Of the Suez canal.


The papers charge the companies with
pooling freight rates and rebating TO con-
Germs that ship exclusively by their lines.
The papers in the suit are in the hands
of United States District Attorney Wise,
who said this afternoon that the suit
would not be entered until next week.


1t was understood that the suit would
be filed today, but at the eleventh hour it
was decided to postpone the filing.


Result of Investigation.


The announcement from New York that
the government will file an antitrust suit
against several of the big steamship COM
panies transporting freight between the
Atlantic coast of the United States to
the far east by the Suez canal comes as
the result of comprehensive investiga-
ton into the general steamship conditions
Alleged pools and agreements covering
other phases of American ocean trade are
being investigated.


The papers prepared for filing allege
ehoe SO'CId1 ui6 SlednSnlp companies
have acquired a complete monopoly of
the transportation of freight between
the United States and the far east by
water.


The action will be brought under the
Sherman antitrust law and will set
forth that by means of agreements,
pools and conferences, freight trade
between the United States and the
Philippines China, Japan and other
countries of the far east has been
mOnopoliZed.


An unlawful combination and conspir-
acy will be alleged through two agree
ments, one cornering the eastward traffic
and the other the westward.


Both the eastward and westward agree
ments, it will be alleged, divide the traf
fc among the defendant companies; that
under the eastward agreement the lines
do not compete at all for government
contracts and the profits are divided and
that deferred rebate system is main
tanned under the westward agreement
Pools are said to exist under both agree
ments into which the earnings of the
steamship lines are placed after the de-
duction of certain expenses.

The floods in the south Atlantic states
caused by the reavy rains of Thursday
and Friday. have proved to be the most
severe since the great floods of August,
1903, especially those in the Savannah
river and the rivers of the Carolinas,
weather bureau officials said last night


In the middle Atlantic states and New
England the floods were more moderate


The effects of the heavy rains also are
being felt in the Ohio river and it's tribu-
taries, and flood warnings have been
issued for the lower Ohio river and the
Tennessee and Wabash rivers. Only a
moderate flood is expected, however, IN
the lower Ohio from the water now in
sight.

streets are almost deserted; President

troops in the NORTH who will obey him,
to re-establish his authority.

disarming looters and paying them few
dollars to return to their homes.

diers to abstain from looting. President
Yuan has issued a proclamation, recit-
ing the duties of the soldiers to the state
and declaring that they should have pride
enough in the profession to maintain their
name.

and Frederick counties. was gratifying
to the organization leaders.

Hail. mighty men who formed the host
That led the nation into light
The nations pride. the nations boast;
An army vanishing from sight.
Repeat your story. from the past.
OF battles lost and battles won.
And files and columns falling fast
Before the sweep of sword and gun.
Tell of your marches. long and drear.
With throats athirst and hlistered feet,
And lips and faces cracked and scar.
With bitter cold or scorchfng heat:
Your thoughts of dear ones. far away.
Who loved and needed you SO much;
The anguish of the bitter day


You left their sight at duty's touch.
No sordid motive was the lure


That took you from your happy home,
The tolls of warfare to endure


To sleep beneath the sky's great dome.
The pittance that the nation gave
Paid lily for your risk of life:
Twas not for that you fought to save
Her honor, through the hateful strife.
The ma ton our forefathers made

In deep distress implored your aid.
Her flag to honored peace to bear.
That nation, to your hearts SO dear,
Was surely worthy to be saved;
And other ties. however near.


Were severed as her foe you braved.
With all the glorious ones that live
And shine through ages of the past,
And light TO present pathways give,
Your host in golden rays shall last;
And in that splendor be revealed,


AS treading still the paths you trod,
And mustered on Fame's stored field,
Reviewed before the throne OF God.

GUAYAQUIL. Ecuador, January 26.-
Gen. Pedro Montero, who recently was
the popular hero of Guayaquil, yesterday
was shot by the angry populace, dragged
into the streets, beheaded and burned.


Gen. Montero in November last was
proclaimed president by the troops sta
toned in Guayaquil. but handed over
the leadership in the provisional govern
ment to Gen. Flavio Alfaro. A revolu-
tionary army went from Guayaquil to
meet the government troops from Quito,
who, under the command of Gen. Leon
idas Plaza, defeated them and eventual
~ forced Guayaquil to capitulate.


Crowd Makes Protest.


Gen. Montero. with other leaders, was
captured January -, and last evening
Gen. Montero was brought before court
martial and sentenced to sixteen years
Imprisonment in penitentiary. When
Gen. Plaza, who presided over the court
of angry people who had surrounded the
government palace awaiting the result
shouted violent protests.


The excitement increased rapidly, and
some of them rushed into the cour r.room,
riddled Gen. Montero with bullets, seized
his body and dragged it into the open
air. There they hacked the head off the
shoulders, gathered fuel with which they
started a fire, and then cast head and
trunk into the flames


Explosion in Barracks.


The excitement lasted throughout the
night, and revolver shooting occurred in
many parts of the city. Gems. Eloy Al
faro and Paez, who were captured at
the same time as Gen. Montero, it is re-
ported. were sent to Quito at midnight.
They will be tried by court-martial in the
capital.


An explosion, occurred in the artillery
barracks here yesterday. Sixty men
were killed or wounded.


Gen. Medardo Alfaro, accompanied by
troops. arrived here yesterday on the
British steamer Quito. He was captured
by the government and imprisoned

NEW YORK, Nov 16.-The cotton mar
6et opened barely steady with prices 3 to
points lower than the closing quotations
OF Friday Later the market turned
strong on the rush OF buying orders and
prices advanced II to 10 points from the
initial figures. The room was taken I'M
prepared for the strong volume of buying
which came from good sources, including
many spot houses and there was a rush
to cover.

fought against the sudden upturn. The
ring was against the market and sold
heavily on all bulges. During the last
half hour a sudden selling wave pre-
vailed which seemed to come from longs
who liquidated heavily Most of those
who were early buyers turned sellers, re-
sulting in a quick decline Of the entire
early advance. The report that Turkey
had refused Bulgar terms, combined with
the favorable weather indications was
said to have been the chief influence for
the disposing of the staple.


At the close the market was steady with
prices to points lower than the final
quotations OF Friday.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


STANTON. Iowa. July 6.-The Burling-
ton railroads westbound fast mail train
made a spectacular dash across burn
ing bridge one mile west Of Stanton yes
terday afternoon and successfully ran the
gantlet Of an obstruction which tied up
the road for six hours. The engineer OF
the mail took the chance OF going through
the burning structure rather than permit
his train to be delayed The bridge, which
spans ravine about fifty feet deep. took
fire from a passing freight. Some time
later the fast mail came up. The engine
came to a stop and the crew went for
ward to reconnoiter. The mail clerks who
manned the eight postal cars of the train
refused to run the gantlet and instead
crossed the ravine on foot. Then the
train backed up, got good start, and
went across the bridge at such high speed
that the paint on the cars was not
scorched.


Trains arriving ten minutes later were
compelled to wait six hours before cross
ing.

along the Wan-Chow river valley,
where the heaviest damage was done.
over 100 towns, villages and hamlets
were wiped out. A number of coast
towns were washed away.

typhoon passed over the province The
hague river is out of its banks, and
thousands of acres of tea has been
washed out.


A big missionary station at Chu

ALEXANDRIA. Va. July . 1912.


When the trial Of Samuel alias Shorty
Allen, colored, was called in the corpora
ton court this morning, and after the
jury had been empaneled and everything
was in readiness to proceed with the case,
Attorney Charles Bendheim, representing
Allen, produced court records to show
that Allen was not the man wanted, and
that the people charged with the muir
der had been tried and convicted


This brought the trial to halt while
juorors and court attaches gasped in as
tonishment A few minutes afterward
Judge Barley Investigated the records
and found that Attorney Bendheim was
right. The court thereupon instructed
the Jury to bring in q verdict of not
guilty against Allen, and this the jury did
without leaving it's box, and Allen went
his way rejoicing.


Allen was indicted for the murder of
Richard Mills colored. which occurred in
this city November i. 1903. Attorney
Benhdeim a few days ago ascertained
from some OF the witnesses that they
were of the opinion that other parties
had already been convicted of the
murder


Before going into court this morning he
looked carefully into the records and
found that Sarah Gaskins and Hugh
King, both colored. at the March term oil
court in 1906. had entered plea OF
guilty to involuntary manslaughter in
connection with the killing of Mills and
were sentenced to serve six months each
in the city Jail. The records also showed
that they were arrested a short time after
Mills had been killed, and were indicted
at the January term of court in 1906.


A similar coincidence in connection with
the case is that the indictments returned
against the man and woman were prac-
tically similar to the one against Allen
who was facing the court In a fight for his
life

the case is the only one Of its character
that has ever before been brought to

BUDAPEST, May 23.-Fierce rioting
broke out this afternoon in the strike
OF employees of public service corpora
tions called by the Social Democratic
party. -Four men were reported killed
and $50 others wounded. Some of the
injured are In such serious condition
that they will probably die.


Rioting broke out during a monster
demonstration when strikers paraded
through the streets, carrying banners.
Soldiers were sent against the rioters
The men and women in the mob fought
back and for time It was feared that
artillery would be necessary to clear
the streets.


The victims were shot to death by
the soldiers who were compelled to fire
several volleys before the frantic riot
ers would disperse. Ten thousand
and for a time handsto hand fighting
ragged In the streets. The scene APP
preached that of revolution.


Street Cars Overturned.


The members of the mob had started
out originally to make a demonstration
by marching before the government
buildings. Singing revolutionary songs
and screaming curses at members of
the government, the marchers paraded
through the principal thoroushfares.
The tumult became so great that the
police tried to clear the streets, but
were unsuccessful. The rioters at
tackled street cars. overturning them
into barricades. Automobiles and car
riages were held up and overturned in
the streets.


The police were bombarded with vol
ley after volley of stones. Filled with
the wanton spirit of violence the rioters
smashed all the windows within sight,
tore down doors and shutters of shops.


Mob Defies Troops.


1t was finally decided to call out the
troops, held in readiness in the bar
racks in anticipation of an outbreak.
Led by cavalry the soldiers marched
through the streets at double quick.
The commander of the soldiers rode
ahead and warned the ringleaders of
the mob that they had better go TO
their homes. They answered with q
volley of bricks and stones.


The order was given to charge and
the cavalrymen urged their horses
against the rioters. Five times the
soldiers charged but were driven back.
They then fired several volleys into the
mob

mere in October with arms and ammuni-

intended for Paraguayan revolutionists.

rifles, a wireless apparatus, uniforms and
other military supplies. There were two
English passengers and five Spanish pas
sengers aboard. Once out OF sight OF
land one Of the Spaniards, Arricos by
name assumed direction Of affairs.


The Zeebrugge. instead of proceeding

had cleared, headed for the mouth Of the

learned 1t was the intention to attack

As soon as the coast was sighted Arri-
COS mounted the guns on deck, the null
of the vessel was repainted and her
name was changed to the Coimbra. Then
the Brazilian. flag was hoisted. Tnanks

was then again changed to the Asun-
cion.


The Belgian crew were compelled 10

with a revolver They feared. too, that
If the vessel were taken they would be
summarily dealt with. They continued.
therefore to work the ship up the river,
during which the vessels name under
went another change, the name Consti-
tucion being painted on her side.

Refusing the invitation Of Arricos 20
ioin his expedition the crew went 10
Buenos Ayres and thence shipped to
Antwerp.

VALDEZ, Alaska, March 3O.-The Alas
ka democratic convention appeared to be
hopelessly divided when the warning fac
tons that separated after stormy ses-
sion last night reassembled their forces
today.


The split had left the convention hall
in possession of the contestants, led by
John Moe Of Fairbanks. The regulars,
who adjourned to another building, car
rying off the credentials of both factions.
worked far into the night over the
proxies from districts from which con-
testing delegates were sent. They claim
to have found evidence that many proxies
from Juneau and elsewhere were forged.


Opening Of Hostilities.


The disturbance began last night when
the territorial committee chairman called
for nominations for temporary chair
man. Moe nominated William OConnor
of Cordova and Judge Cobb of Juneau
named Edmund Smith CT Valdez.


A bitter exchange of personalities en-
sued. and when the tumult was at its
height Moe called for a viva voce vote
and declared OConnor elected


This announcement precipitated a rush
to seize the chair and take the creden-
tails from the committee secretary.

MANILA. October 19.-Twenty- five
million dollars is the estimated damage
done by the typhoon that swept the
Philippines October 18. The storm
extended over a wide area, touching
Surigao in the south. Taoloban in the
north and crossing Leyte. Bohol. Cebu.
Negroes and Panay.


Reports from the various districts are
incomplete. and contain nothing def
mite concerning the rich sugar district
in Negroes, nor the interior points in
Cebu and Panay.


Five small coasting steamers were
driven ashore and wrecked, and hun
dred small sailing vessels were sunk or
beached.


Army and Navy Helping.


The army and navy have both Joined
the government in undertaking measures
Of relief. Rear Admiral r. F. Nicholson.
commander Of the United States Asiatic
fleet, has placed the cruiser Cincinnati
at the service of the government. and
has gone south with Brig. Gen. Harry N.
BandholtZ chief Of the Philippine con-
stabulary. The army authorities are
lending doctors and men of the hospital
corps together with tents.


The government is dispatching one
other with supplies of food. while 1t Is
holding the transport Warren in reserve.


Apparently there were no casualties
among American residents. The total
number of dead among the natives has
not yet been ascertained.

breakers were severely beaten. There

day fully 5000 persons have been con-
gregated in Broad street.

ing on special train and patrols were
soon stationed on every street in the
downtown and factory districts. The
presence of the military has apparently
quelled the rioting.

long struggle following the repeated at
tempts made last night to dynamite
street cars throughout Greater Boston,

Labor Union will call out 5000 work.
Ing men In every branch Of trade in q
general sympathetic strike unless the
new union Of elevated employees is given

Shortly before midnight last night q
Watertown car, just before IL reached
the Brighton Bridge, was wrecked by a
powerful charge Of dynamite which
shattered every window, ripped the
flooring and wood work into splinters
and narrowly escaped seriously injuring
motorman, conductor and one passen-
ger which the car contained.


More Dynamite Found.


Less than ten feet away q quantity
Of dynamite Weighing about a pound,
was found and If this had been explod-
ed the results would have been disas-
trous to the neighborhood.


A general alarm was sounded, and
about half an hour later four sticks
Of dynamite were found on the tracks
near the Watertown Arsenal Just before
a crowded night car came speeding
along.


Rumors are current that dynamite
was found early today In several other
sections of the suburbs, but II Is said
the officials of the company are keep
Ing the facts suppressed in order to
prevent a complete panic throughout
the Boston district.
Rioting Through Night.


There was much petty rioting
throughout the city all night, several
rike-breakers being reported injured,
but only one arrest was made.


Today conditions are quiet, with all
police reserves and plain clothes men
covering the districts where trouble is
likely to break out.

SCRANTON. Pa, May 1O.-Cayuga
breaker of the Delaware, Lackawanna
and Western Company, in North Scranton,
formed the background Of an ugly riot
GUS demonstration today. Foreign work
men were leaders among the crowd of
1000 men and boys that assembled near
the breaker to keep away men who were
going to the necessary work. They were
wild in their outcries and defied the
squad Of local police. who had an hour
before been ordered out from every sta
ton on notice from the mine officials that
trouble was threatened. The idle work
ers broke through the police lines, rush.
ed the firerooms and dragged out men,
turning them over to others who beat
them and threw them aside.


Several Are Injured.


State police on duty all night at the
Leggetts Creek mine, a mile away, hur-
ried over, and their coming rallied the
local police and together the officers
charged the mob. There were shots from
the rioters Bricks stones and clubs
were thrown and the officers, dropping
their clubs, drew their guns and began
to force the crowd back.


Some shots were fired by the police as
Policemen Peter Marker and Louis Davis
fell, both with battered heads from
cobblestones. The state troopers then
rode into the crowd, firing their revolvers
Mike Flacka and another foreigner drop
ped to the ground, the former shot
through the abdomen. the latter in the
leg. The crowd then broke and ran. and
the police combined to drive them on to-
ward the houses.


Women Also Arrested.


Two men and a half dozen women were
arrested.


The rioters took refuge behind cars on
the railroad near the breaker. but were
finally dispersed when the railroad police
came up on q special car and began to
hand out guns to the local policemen
Capt Williams and Director O'Malloy of
the Scranton department Of public safety
ordered the police to patrol the entire
grounds and to suppress at once any
further trouble. They also warned the
crowd OF people. many Of whom were at
tracted to the place by the trouble, to
disperse, telling them to remain away
and stay peaceable.


The foreigners threatened all kinds of
trouble, but the police and troopers now
seem to have the situation under control
William Lttlejohn, going to fire duty at
the Leggetts Creek mine. was badly
beaten by women.

the cheering was over Major General
Organ made AN announcement that
brought even gre alter applause. This was
that on August the New York militia
would go over into Connecticut and have

meg State.

ously that he might see the members of

brief. but Harrington died with a smile
on his face.

NEW HAVEN, Conn, May 24.-Mem-
bers of the three senior secret societies
at Yale were locked out Of their rooms
early today by students of the senior
class not members Of the fraternities,
and were forced to submit to taunts and
jeers outside the gate at the entrance to
Vanderbilt Hall on the campus, while
those inside the Enclosure danced around
a big bonfire on which was piled furni-
ture. bedding and any other material
which came handy.


The senior societies meet Thursday
evenings and the members leave the
chapter houses shortly after midnight;
The appearance of the fraternity men at
Vanderbilt courtyard was the signal for
the other students gathered there to start
the bonfire and close the gates.


Climb Over Glued Gates.


The fraternity men after futile attempts
to enter their dormitories by ladders
placed at the windows were forced to
climb over the iron gates, which had been
covered with thick glue. Only one ex-
ception was made. Scroll and Keys man
being allowed to get into his room. For
nearly two hours they were kept outside,
when they were requested by the seniors
inside the Enclosure to climb over the
gate, one man at a time, as his name
was called.


While the demonstration was in prog
ress Dean Frederick s. Jones Of the
academic department. appeared on the
scene and asked the men to desist. No
attention was paid to his request, how
ever.


Coming closely after the recent mock
tap day" ceremony on the Yale campus
which preceded the annual ceremony by
one day, this latest demonstration was
the subject of excited comment about the
campus today.

The task of overhauling a legal code

had any thoroughgoing revision since

have similarly gone without recasting. In
this case practice has shown the need OF
reform beyond all question. Gen. Crowter
declares that the administration Of justice

from which ours were largely taken. have
been revised. through the medium of the
annual army act, until they bear but lit
tie resemblance to the originals. But
ours remain antiquated in parts.

ice is clear enough. Like many of our
army customs. the articles were taken
over bodily in ITS, the Continental Con-
gress November Z adding sixteen provis-
ions Ii deemed necessary. This code was
revised in 1916, and under II the revolu-
ton was fought.

NEW YORK, February 15.-Twenty-
five thousand dollars in currency was
stolen from taxicab in the heart of the
financial district this morning by three
highwaymen who sprang into the vehicle
and overpowered w. F. Smith and Frank
Wardell, messengers of the East River
National Bank. at $50 Broadway. Both
messengers were badly injured, and the
robbers escaped with the money-$15, 600
In five-dollar bills and $4,000 in one
hundred-dollar bills. The currency was
being transported from the Produce Ex-
change Bank, in the lower part of the
city.


The taxicab had proceeded up Broad
way without mishap when, for some un-
explained reason, the chaffeur turned
west on Rector street into Church street,
skirting the side and rear of Trinity
churchyard.


Three Jump Into Taxi.


About midway Of the old cemetery
three men sprang from the curb. One
jumped on the chauffeur's seat, the other
two got into the vehicle. The man on the
seat pressed revolver in his overcoat
pocket against the side OF the chauffeur.
Gino Martini, and commanded him to
drive swiftly on without making an out
cry.


Inside the vehicle the two robbers were
belaboring the bank messengers over the
head. Smith, one Of the messengers, is
siXty-one years old, and he was bleeding
and almost unconscious when the taxicab
reached Park place, few blocks north.
Wardell was badly beaten about the head,
but not so seriously hurt.


Escape in Waiting Auto.


At Park place the highwaymen jumped
from the taXicab, bearing a tin box. which
they had wrested from the messengers
and which contained the currency. In
flash they had sprung into a big black
automobile, which seemed to be awaiting
their coming. and were quickly lost in
the mass of traffic.


Martini, the taxicab chauffeur, contin-
ued to run his machine until he found
policeman. Here he gave the alarm, and
the two injured messengers were taken
to police station. Smiths condition was
Wardells scalp was badly. lacerated. but
because of his youth he stood the fight
well.


Fail to Rob Jewelry Store.


Hold-ups and money-snatching games
have become almost epidemic in New
York in the past few weeks Preceding
today's taxicab affair by scarcely an hour,
two young men armed with revolvers at
tempted to rob the jewelry establishment
of Barrett Nemets on Broome street. The
jeweler showed fight, grappled with the
intruders. and, when they fed, fired sew
eral shots at them, which were returned.
One of the men escaped, the other was
captured He gave the name of Max
Silver, seventeen years old. A revolver
with five exploded cartridges in the cyl
inder was found in his pocket

ied the selling movement. However,

call the general option list rallied within
about points from the opening.

Singley. surgeon at the Childrens Hos
pital, is receiving congratulations OF the
medical profession here on series OF
remarkable operations that practically
rebuilt Agnes Ober. five years old. The
child left the hospital today walking
for the first time in her life. except for
the practicing she had done in the ward
where she had been for six months.


The girl was born cripple. Her
spine was crooked and her limbs were
powerless. The spine curvature was
remedled and then the hips and knees
were dislocated and reset. Agnes body
was put IN a plaster cast and her legs
IN steel braces These have been re-
moved. and surgeons who examined her
say that after she RECEIVERS her strength
she will be a normal. healthy child.

Standardization OF the pleasure types
of cars and the advancement and develop
ment in efficiency and refinement are the
real reasons for the present day informed
attitude OF the automobile-using public.
Just as soon as the motor car demon
strated it's practicability, the general pub
lie began to try to learn something about
it. The result has been that the public
has advanced with the advance of the
automobile, until today both have reached
a satisfactory state. The motor car is
well along toward freedom from faults,
and the owners have mastered nearly all
its perplexities.


The pioneers of car making have not in
the last several years made material
changes in one years design from an
other and this season the only addition
to some leading cars is more complete
equipment and in some cases the adop-
ton of a particular type of self-starter.


For the last three or four years auto
mobile manufacturers have devoted their
attention to the development of luxury,
refinement and comfort for the user Spa
cious seating room. good upholstering,
highly polished paint and many other de-
tails of appointment are the chief fea
lures OF the motor car of today. The
lighting problem has been solved by the
installation of an electric dynamo, by
which is generated electricity for lighting
the outside lamps and generally at the
same time furnishing the power for self
starters. The electric lighting system is
several years old. but II has reached it's
highest degree of perfection only this
year.


Another important Improvement this
year, and one that will particularly inter
est the motorist, is increased baggage
equipment. Almost every car. large or
small, has provided for carrying extra
luggage. More and more such equipment
has been necessary because of the motor
lists desire to tour through the country
for weekend trips. and often cross-con-
tinent touring for three and four weeks
at a time.

AUGUSTA, GA. July 1.-Two prom
inent farmers Of Richmond county came
very near meeting death by cremation
last night when the garage. automobile,
barns and stables OF c. NJ. Rhodes were
burned Mr.. Rhodes lives six miles
from the city on the Washington road.
Accompanied by his wife and children
and his wife's uncle, Louis Atkins, he
went for an auto ride, returning after
nightfali.


Mrs. Rhodes and the children were
left at the residence and Messrs. Rhodes
and Atkins drove the automobile into
the garage. The place had only one
door and as soon as the automobile got
inside the wind blew the door shut, up
setting a kerosene lamp, which ignited
everything around It, The two men
were trapped. the only means of escape
being through the flames They finally
got out, although both were badly
burned


Fifteen horses and mules and a num-
Der of hogs were saved. but several
hundred bushels of corn and oats were
consumed. A female hound dog with
half dozen puppies died with her off
spring rather than leave them The
puppies were too small to walk

The fifth international congress of chambers of
commerce will assemble next week for its first Amer
ican meeting


These international commercial and other unions
are of comparatively recent growth 1t was not So
long since that the banding together of business men
representative of competitive nations would have
been considered an impossibility. The first inter-
national congress of chambers of commerce, for ex-
ample, occurred in Belgium but eight years ago.
Today nearly 500 men, representing forty-seven diff
ferent countries, will participate. The idea that the
different peoples could find common meeting
ground has been destroyed.


There have been four of these biennial con-
crosses, the first at Liege, Belgium, the second at
Milan, the third in Prague, and the fourth in London.
The keynote Of these gatherings has been that the
business of the nations, welded together should
impress upon the world the dignity and the power
of commerce and the determination of business men
that ,trade-national and inernational-be purified
the world around.

PHILADELPHIA, February 17.-Al-
though both are dying and know it.
George Sicler of Germantown and his
bride. who prior to last Saturday was
Miss Genevieve Laurente of Pittsburgh,
say they are happy. On adjoining cots
In the Dermady Cottage Sanatorium,
at Morton, Pa, they are awaiting death,
Both are incurable victims of the
white plague" and both are in it's
final grip.


The romance which terminated in
their marriage last Saturday, when
their cots were pulled close together
SO that the dying man might place the
ring on the finger of his dying fiancee
while the Rev. George Wilson perform
ed the marriage ceremony, began seven
years ago, when Sicler, to all appear
ances a hale and hearty man, was or
dered to Mount Airy. The physicians
had discovered the little germ in one
lung, which has spread until both lungs
are now nearly gone.


Girl Became His Nurse.


At Mount Airy he met and fell in love
with Miss Laurente. She was q rudy
complexioned, healthy girl. and she en-
deavored to nurse the man back to
health. In nursing him she contracted
tuberculosis. She wilted and faded into
a living skeleton. Her condition kept
pace with his.


For three years they have occupied
adjoining cots. each endeavoring to
cheer the other.


Hemorrhage followed hemorrhage,
each more severe than the preceding
one. When the man had one of the
terrible attacks the woman invariably
followed with another They apparently
were dying at the same pace.


Last Saturday, after terrible cough
ing spells, they decided to die as man
and wife. The two cots were placed
close together and the sad ceremony
was performed. Now Mr.. and Mrs.
sicler are awaiting the call to a higher
altar.

turbances early to-day two persons were
drowned and scores were made homeless

reads and trolley traffic was stopped and
roads and bridges were washed away.

foundations. Fowler and his six children
were in the house. Margaret. aged nine,

track from Eighty-four to Washington.

days, reached Philadelphia yesterday

The men, William Buck and Frank
Alden, shipped on the smack Confidence,
out Of Gloucester. Two weeks ago it had
many barrels Of cod sailed away, and
it was on it's last day before the run
back to Gloucester that Buck and Alden
got lost in the fog.


Sailors Become Lost.


All that day and the next night they
pulled the dory and shouted for help but
at last admitted to each other that they
were lost. A few biscuits and a gallon
can of water were all the provisions they
had on board, and it went the first day.

thick, and they stopped rowing to save
their strength when the last biscuit went.

ing in fish and eating them raw. But

salt almost drove them mad with thirst.


Before dawn of the third day a gale

away the fog and driving them north of

craft

Those fans of the gridiron sport who
know the rules and the various changes
which take place in them from year to
year were disappointed in their hopes
of seeing them put to the test in Sat
urday's game between the Eleventh
cavalry and the yellow Jacket teams.


Straight football was used almost
entirely. and the old style line plays
we're very much in evidence they being
used by both sides to no advantage,
neither side putting the ball across in
the entire game.


The field was wet and heavy, and the
hall was thoroughly soaked, and there
fore the forward pass was not used to
any advantage and trick plays were out
of the question, as such plays require
fast handling of the ball and accurate
passing, and neither was possible un-
der the conditions.


Everything being considered, Tech
should have had the game, and would
have had it if just a little more head
work had been used at the right time
Techs bucking was extra good, COlley
and Leuhrman going for good gains
nearly every time called The back
field also did fairly good work in this
respect, but as they had to wait until
the ball was caught before getting a
start, they were necessarily hindered
and on this account the end runs were
not up to their usual value. twas ex-
tremely hard for the interference to
form under the weather conditions. and
being so heavily outweighed, the in
reference was of little value and the
man with the ball was generally down
ed before he got started good,


Fumbling was Also very noticeable

A coroner's jury yesterday discharged
Frederick Heyl, chauffeur for Simon b.
Eisendrath, who was charged with run
ming over and killing Patrick Fay. a
seven year-old boy. at No. II West End
avenue. Heyl was arrested three days
after the boys death and formally
charged with homicide, and Eisendrath,
who was said TO have been in the auto
mobile at the time, was held as an ac-
cessory.


Coroner Hellenstein discharged Eisen-
drath yesterday before he called any
witnesses. The Coroner said the police
had failed to produce any evidence that
would warrant holding the architect.


John Lowry and Thomas Lorenz, two
of Fay's playmates, were examined. and
Lorenz told of getting the cars number
as it sped away after striking the Fay
boy. Thomas Parent, driver also got
the number of the car, and Detective
James Mccormick told of tracing the car
from the number given.


The Coroner told the jury to hold Heyl
If they thought him guilty of careless or
negligent driving. The jury was out
twenty minutes, and said the accident
was unavoidable. Both Heyl and Eisen-
drath were discharged.

through weak bull spectators unloading

lowed.

tween Italy and Turkey and growing
belief that the powers will prevent the
threatened outbreak in the Balkans Gre
ated a more confident feeling here as
we'll as on the continental bourses at the
end Of the week, and much stock was re-
purchased and earlier losses reduced, al
though the situation is still sufficiently
unsettled to check any large expansion in
Consols were not affected by the crisis
and closed practically unchanged.


American Securities Depressed.

pressed early by continental selling and,
although favorable trade and harvest
prospects made a stronger market and





a good recovery in the middle of the
week, today's setback, in sympathy with

slower and slower, and the little fellow
fell fast asleep.


The next morning Robs mother found

marks, which he claimed TO be stars.

Baltimore, Oct. 20-Joseph Whitney.
president Of the Merchants and Miners
Steamship Company, stated to-day
that he had received word from Cap
tain Hart that all the passengers
aboard the steamer Berkshire, bound
from Savannah to Philadelphia, which
is on fire about forty-three miles north
east Of Cape Lookout, were safe aboard
the steamer and that the fire. confined
10 the forward hold, was under control.
At the company's main Offices In this
city only few short messages had
been received from Captain Hart.


The fire. according to dispatches from
special correspondents, was discovered
about midnight In the lower forward
hold. The Berkshire was then some
distance from the coast, rolling and
tossing and making only fair Roadway
against the head winds. When the fire
was reported to the captain he real
lied Immediately the necessity Of get
ting 10 shore as quickly as possible.
Ordering all the matches battened down,
he had the wireless operator send out
the distress call, and Immediately
turned the ships nose toward the
slight harbor back Of Cape Lookout, to
which mariners give the name Lookout
Cove.


Three vessels answered the call al
most Immediately. They were the Gre
tan, Of the same line, which left Balti-
more on Friday evening for Savannah;


the Apache of the clyde Line, and an


other vessel Of whose identity the off,


Gals here are not certain.


The Apache was the nearest vessel


and soon came in sight Of the burning


liner. The Cretan followed, and both


stood by to offer what assistance they
could. It was o'clock when the
Apache reached the side Of the Berk-
shire. Two hours later the vessel
dropped anchor in the less turbulen.


waters Of the cove, the other two ships


Immediately behind her.


The men passengers worked with the
| crew in subduing the flames and in
preventing the fire from spreading. A
| late dispatch said the steamer was not
seriously damaged. For a time the
women passengers were alarmed, but
confidence was soon restored.


The Merchants and Miners has been
particularly unfortunate in the last
year or 50, several vessels having been
destroyed or badly injured. The Nam
tucket was the last vessel to be burned.
On September 2 she took fire at her
pier at Locust Point and sank. The
Ontario took fire off Montauk Point last
spring and was beached Her rebuild
ing is being completed. A year or


more ago another steamer was wrecked


at the mouth OF the st. Johns River, in
Florida, and the Essex burned at her
dock only two or three years before.

Capt. H. E. Honeywell and Roy F.
Donaldson. the balloonists who won the
elimination race from Kansas City. left
Washington to return home over the
Pennsylvania Railroad at 6:45 O'Clock
yesterday evening.


The balloon Uncle Sam" covered about
l.25O miles in making the trip from Kan
sas City to the field near Manassas, Va,
where the aeronauts landed. although the
direct distance is only about $50 miles.
The journey required thirty-five hours.
and during that period neither Of the
men was able to take more than few
minutes of sleep at a time. They also
suffered severely from the heat, which
beats down with great intensity in the
rarefied atmosphere at high elevations.
The wonderful views seen by moonlight
among the clouds more than repaid them
for all suffering, however. according to
Capt. Honeywelrs statement.


These men will represent the United
States in the international balloon race.
which starts from Stuttgart, Germany,
October 26.

NEW YORK, June 26.-The marriage of

place at Mrs. Amsinck's town house, $40
9Th avenue. in the drawing room. on the
second floor, looking out over the park
The room was decorated with white roses
and palms The Very Rev. Dean Gros-
venor of the Cathedral of St. John the
Divine ofhciated, the ceremony taking
place at o'clock. The bride wore a sof,
gray gown. topped by a matching hat
and there were no attendants. Those ip-
vited included the families and very close
friends of Mr.. Fish and his bride. less
than fifty in all A breakfast, but no re-
ception. followed, the tables being deco
rated with roses. Pink and white roses
and palms were used throughout the wide
main hall and dining room.


Mr.. and Mrs. Fish left during the after
July will sail for Europe to travel there
by motor They will visit Italy and be fol
a time at Mrs. Fish's villa. Their stay
abroad will be indefinite, perhaps only
six months and perhaps eighteen.

United States under President Roosevelt
and representative for seveal years

Albany. who died twelve years ago. He
has four daughters, Mrs. w. L. Breese
and Mrs. John H. Cutler of Boston, and
the Misses Janet and Helen Fish, and
one son, Hamilton Fish. jr.


Mrs. Fish was formerly Miss Florence
Delaplaine, and married. frst, James Hude
Beekman. who died several years since
She then married Gustave Amsinck, q
well known banker and bachelor, who
died two years ago.

But your mothers life has not been
easy. Your father was a poor man. and
from the day she married him she stood
by his side. fighting the wolf from the
door with her naked hands, as a woman
must fight.


She worked not the eight or ten-hour
day of the union. but the twenty-four-
hour day of the poor wife and mother.


She cooked and cleaned and scrubbed
and patched and nursed from dawn un-
til bedtime. and in the night was up and
down getting drinks for thirsty lips,
covering restless little sleepers, listening
for croupy coughs.


She had time to listen to your stories
of boyish fun and frOlic and triumph


She had time to say the things that
spurred your ambition on.


She never forgot to cook the little
dishes you liked.


She did without the dress she needed
that you might not be ashamed OF your
clothes before your fellows.


Remember this now while there is yet
time. while she is living. TO pay back
to her in love and tenderness some of
the debt you owe her. You can never
pay 1: all, but pay down something in
account this very night.

Once the pride of the United States
navy. the receiving ship Wabash. known
as "Old Homestead" stationed at the
Boston Navy Yard for thirty-seven years
has been condemned for naval purposes
and shortly will be consigned to the scrap
heap She is the sole survivor of the
quintet of ships which marked the advent
of steam propulsion for warships. The
historic Merrimac, Minnesota, Colorado
and Roanoke. which were sister ships
have passed away.


The Wabash was first commissioned in
1886 at Philadelphia. where she was built
Like her sister ships, she was designed
to combine auxiliary steam power with
a heavy sail plan. the first practical
introduction of steam propulsion in navy
vessels of lighting size. She was first the
flagship of Flag Officer Hiram Paulding
and, like her sister vessels, went abroad
and was highly complimented by the eX-
tensive copies made of her throughout
the entire naval world.

asleep before o'clock.

declared that they had already won

NEWPORT NEWS, Va, February 8.
Twenty days overdue and with only the
wooden fittings of the ship for fuel dur
ing the last two days" run, the British
steamer Bracondate arrived here in dis
tress yesterday afternoon after one of
the toughest voyages reported in years.
The steamer left Volo, Greece. cargo
laden for Philadelphia, December -.
After passing Gibraltar she encountered
high winds and rough seas, and for six
teen consecutive days labored in the
teeth of a strong head gale. Tuesday
morning, while 800 miles east-southeast
Of Cape Henry, the coal supply became
completely exhausted, and all Of Tuesday,
Tuesday night and yesterday morning
out and cutting up bulkheads, grain
partitions, ladders, fittings and frame
work. This was used for fuel, but the
best efforts of the crew resulted In get
ting a speed of from only three to five
knots out of the engines in a calm sea,
the first good weather of the trip. When
the ship entered port the supply was ex-
hausted, and before the ship could be
locked the fires were out. Capt Allen
said last night that the trip was the
worst in his sea experience, and that but
for the fact Of calm weather Tuesday

have reached port. Even the cabin and
galley fires had to be extinguished for
economy.

BALTIMORE, July 3.-Baltimore is
the city of the exodus today. 1t is the
dlsmantled stage of checked political
ambitions, hopes that fed overnight, de-
serted campaign headquarters, collapsed
booms, dropping banners, and jobless
press agents.


The Democratic convention OF 1912 has
passed into history. The station gates
clang behind the departing visitors; the
delegates and other participants in a
memorable struggle drop dejectedly into
the seat Of Pullman car and start the
long journey homeward. Some wear the
badges and the campaign insignia which
bedecked them when they came. The
majority of them have pocketed their
decorations or else have changed the
old button for the new. There were a
dozen candidates, and only one reached
the goal of his ambition. The disappear
ing ones are for the winner-for he's
Democrat-but there still fingers with
the disappointed the thought of the
might have been.


The convention city will be itself again
within the next twenty-four hours. The
hotel lobbies are disgorging the crowds
which have made them place OF bed





which once hung from ceilings and walls
have been swept into the gutter. On the
streets is scattered the refuse of the
carnival crowds-literature extolling the
virtues of "favorite son." pennant
or so, and the confetti remnants of a
wild night.


Street Fakers Gone.


One misses now the rasping voice OF
the street faker, who was a Democrat
for a week. He's gone, with his value
less stock in trade. The "newsies" cry
no extra papers and ribald laughter and
cheers do not float from the corner
cafe.


The "houn' dawg'' sinks down the
alley, dreading another kick from Bryan
and he's followed by Murphy's goat
Over at Convention Hall a half hun
dred men are sweeping out the debris.
Here there was presented for a week a
political drama which will live always ,,
in the memory of those who witnessed
it's climaxes and its final curtain. The
old place lacks life today, however and
Convention Hall signifies only build
of wood and stone.
The hotels present the same scene of
comparative desolation. When the nom-
ination was made yesterday men be-
gan to go silently through the corridors



pictures, the fags, and the notices
which have greeted the eye for nearly
two weeks.


The% bewhiskered countenance OF
Mayor Gaynor no longer peers around a
marble pillar; the stalwart form of Gov
ernor Harmon and the inscription: He
carried Ohio by 100, 000," isn't represent
ed at the head of the stairway; the i'm
mense photograph of Champ Clark
SOSTR Snt Sorn fSSe the osC.r %s aGdrwtns Gd the
doesn't even lend its benedicton to the
And the press agents, where are they?
They have folded their typewriter cases
and silently stolen away. The mimeo-
graph Is giving a rest to the overworked
wax sheets; there are no reams of free
copy: there are no stories of epochal
conferences and midnight trades, and
nobody draws one aside to predict that
tomorrow something will happen.


It's All Over.
It has already happened. The conven-
tton aftermath is here Baltimore is
becoming normal and its hysteria is
passing. Prices in the hotels the bars,
and the cafes are seeking their level.
The rented cots are being returned to
real bed may be had without hypothe-
eating ones earthly possessions. and
meal may be eaten without interruption
by roll call.


For a few days Baltimore will miss
the crowds, and the crowds will miss
the fight he precipitated, everybody got
used to one another before the end A
few more ballots and Baltimore might
have advertised the convention as
summer stock production, playing to
crowded houses.
