sengers of the stranded steamship Tur-
rialba. about sixty in all, We're safely
transferred shortly before 3 o'clock this
morning to the revenue cutter Seneca
The Seneca started Immediately for New
York.


News of the transfer came in a wire
less message from Capt. Lindsay COM
mander of the Turrialba, to the United
Fruit Company offices here. "All pas
sengers safely transferred to Seneca
said the message. ship lying easy and
making no water"


The Seneca should reach New York
some time this afternoon.


After all the day and night before
Christmas on board the Turrialba, ashore
nine miles north of Atlantic City, N. j..
the passengers were waiting early this
morning to be transferred to the Seneca
or to be taken off and landed by the
life savers. At daybreak the big steel
vessel was still dry throughout, the
weather was fine and the sea moderate.


Shortly before O. clock word came from
the Brigantine life-saving station that its
crew was aboard the stranded steamer,
with the Seneca standing by, and it was
believed the passengers would be taken
OFF without great difficulty and perhaps
reach New York before Christmas day
had closed.

PHILADELPHIA. December 2j.-The
British steamships Merton and the Oceano.
which were IN collision last night in the
Delaware bay, reached Philadelphia to-
day apparently not badly damaged. The
Merton, carrying passengers as well as
freight left here yesterday for Liverpool.
The passengers showed but little excite
ment after the collision and nearly all Of
them were asleep in their berths when the
steamship arrived back in port. They
probably will be sent to Europe on a
boat sailing from New York. The Oceano
was inbound. bound from Marvik for
Philadelphia. loaded with iron. Both boats
will be surveyed in order that the extent
of the damage may be ascertained.

PARIS, May 3O.-Fez, the Moroccan
capital. Is practically surrounded by hos
tile Moors. according to wireless advices
received by the French government from
Gen. Lyautey. French resident governor,
under date of May %.


Gen. Lyautey says the situation con-
tinues serious. Although a battery Of
French artillery Is due to arrive tomor-
row to reinforce the garrison, the French
troops are still in insufficient numbers to
undertake a decisive offensive sortie from
the city, although capable of holding the
capital against attack


On the afternoon of May 2S the general
reports, the Arabs again fought their way
within the walls of the city, but the
French troops. who had been under arms
almost necessarily for five days, quickly
repulsed them. The Arabs left thirty
dead on the field and undoubtedly carried
off many more. The French lost five SOL
diers killed and eight wounded. In the
course of the earlier fighting the French
casualties numbered sixty wounded.


The Sultan of Morocco had shown signs
of being panic stricken, but has become
reassured since he finds that the popu-
lation of Fez is not joining the attack.

Albany, Nov. 21.-Just before leaving

ernor Dix announced that he had par
doned Albert 7. Patrick, who was
under life sentence at Sing Sing Prison
for the murder Of William Marsh Rice,
an aged millionaire, in New York City
on September %, 1900.


For some time the Governor has been
considering the case of Patrick, AMI
had gone over carefully the letters re-
ceived from prominent persons all over
the country asking that the condemned
man be given his liberty. Like all
victiOn, the present Chief Executive re-
ceiyed an application for pardon from
the prisoner himself. Governor Dix
refused TO give out any of the names
of the persons asking for clemency for
Patrick, saying he considered them ~
the nature of personal communications,
and that the writer's would not like to
have their names made public: The

There has always been an air OF rys.
terry in this important case. Quoting
from The minority opinion, the atnno-
sphere that surrounded the defendant
showed that fair and impartial trial
was scarcely possible.


! trust that Mr.. Patrick will devote
his energies to complete vindication
OF his declared innocence. During the
last year | have given much considers
ton 10 this case. and am conVinced that
the defendant is entitled to have full
pardon.


Patrick, who was saved from the
electric chair by the late Governor Hig-
gins. in December, 1906, has made a
remarkable fight for freedom. A law
yer, he protested when Governor Hig-
gins commuted the death sentence to
life imprisonment, declaring the Gov
ernor had no legal right to cancel the
original sentence and impose a punish
mcnt of life Imprisonment

Scott. Superintendent Of State Prisons,

Patrick's pardon.

DOUGLAS, Ariz.. Aug. S.-That two
Americans have been added to the list
of foreigners supposedly murdered In
Mexico was the belief here today of
friends of Cordio and K. Boyd.


Friends of the Boyd brothers reached
Douglas today from the Carretas ranch.
twenty-six miles east of Colonia,
Oaxaca. They reported that the broth
ers had been living on the ranch with
their father, ]. J. Boyd.and had not been
seen since July 3O Their house later
was found wide-open and deserted.
Lying about It and inside were nearly
400 empty cartridges. showing marks Of
recent use.


The matter was reported to General
Sanjines, who sent one OF his officers
to investigate. The officer confirmed
the report here of the brothers disap-
pearance. and added that their father
and their Chinese cook were also miss
ing.

New York. Aug. 1s.-Mel Shappard.
James F. Meredith. and Donald Lippin-
colt. noted athletes and members OF the
winning American team at Stockholm.
are stranded in Glasgow, without funds
with which TO engage passage home. and
in such circumstances that they will be
compelled to find jobs on the other side
unless financial aid comes from friends
over here.


This report was brought to New York
by the purser OF the steamship Caledonia.
which arrived to-day. According to the
purser. the three athletes went aboard
the Caledonia, expecting to return On
her, but were shown that the return
tickets furnished them were not good
after August 10. They were unable to
scrape together the passage money and
had to stay behind


The purser said the athletes had been
competing in athletic meets in Scottish
towns for several days, but could not
take money for that work because they
are amateurs.

MUSKOGEE, Okla. October 90
Three youthful robbers held up a
southbound Missouri, Kansas and
Texas train. south of Eufaula today
compelled the engineer to detach the
express and baggage cars and run them
ahead then they blasted and rified the
express safe. Company officials be-
lieve the robbers got several thousand
dollars.


BY setting fire to a trestle near the
town of Wirth, the bandits had no
trouble in tagging the train to
halt


Deliberate in Movements.


Although the flames threatened to
destroy the trestle before their work
was accomplished the robbers moved
deliberately Covering the engineer
and fireman with their revolvers. they
ordered them from the locomotive cab.
]. A. Dolan, the trains conductor.
leaped from a coach and he was lined
up beside the enginemen. A porter
also fell a victim to his curiosity. and
was made to stand beside the con-
ductor.


While one robber held the line of en-
ployes the two others uncoupled the en-
gine. baggage and express car from the
coaches. They then forced the trainmen





open the throttle.


Cross Burning Bridge.


The locomotive, pulling the two cars,
shot across the burning bridge. What
remained of the structure fell into the
water a minute after the cars had passed.
The passenger coaches were left stand
ing at the brink of the stream.


Half mile on the other side of the
bridge the bandits ordered the engineer
to step. The safe in the express car was
dynamited and ransacked.
Their work completed, the robbers fled
to the wood-covered hills with their
plunder


The alarm was soon given and posses
were sent from Cyowder and Eufaula.
Other posses left an hour later on special
trains from McAlester and Muskogee.
According to the descriptions given, each
of the bandits was less than twenty-five
years old.

The briar which furnishes the root

shrub called the white heath. or
heather. and Is found chiefly In the
south OF Italy. on the island of Cor
sica. and In Algeria. The shrub often
grows to n large size. although only
the roots are used In the pipe-making
industry.


After the roots have been cleaned of
the earth which clings to them. they
are sawed into blocks of various dimen-

simmer for twelve hours, which brings
out the rich brown color for which the
finest pipes are priced

blocks are steam dried for two weeks.

they are converted into pipes. The
blocks are sorted according to size by
experts. are placed on shelves and kept
at an even temperature for ten days.
when they are dried. and then are sent
to the machines, where the actual man.
ufacture begins. After the blocks have
been trimmed to the proper size, the

are sandpapered. The finishing OF the

San Francisco has just celebrated the

earthquake and FIRE. On the very morn

first details of the Titanic tragedy the
Golden Gate was holding exercises in
observance of its own catastrophe a
scant half dozen years before. She has
risen from her ashes, and her eyes are
pointing toward the future


With the characteristic spirit of her
Argonaut pioneers, San Francisco has
not only surmounted all visible results
from her ordeal, but is making greater
progress than ever before. Six months
after the earthquake and fire the re-
building was well under way. Three
years afterward practically all traces of
the disaster had disappeared from the
city. Five years afterward the city had
selected site for a great international
exposition, and had given satisfactory
assurances to Congress of its ability to
raise on its own account $I5,ooo,ooo to-
ward forwarding the enterprise.


San Francisco hopes for unexampled
growth after the completion of the
Panama Canal She is not thinking
of her tragedy of six years ago; that
has simply made her ambition all the
more unconquerable. Her high spirit
sets an example to all the cities of the
world.

Indiana Harbor. Ind. Nov. n.-Police
and representatives of the Great Lakes
Dredge and Dock Company are dragging
the harbor here for the bodies of three
of four men drowned when the ore
steamer Goulder, rammed and sunk the
tug William A. Field. last night. The
Field was towing a big empty freighter
out OF the Indiana Steel Company docks.
The big vessel was evidently caught by
the brisk lake breeze and was borne
down toward one Of the harbor sand
bars. The tug tried to. pass under her
bows, was caught by the overhang and
pushed down under the water. Five
men were aboard. One was rescued and
the body of one other recovered.

amendment was attached repeating all
but the pulp and paper section of the
Canadian reciprocity law.

the Senate and reposed with the
wool bill among the papers technically
ON the desk of the President of the

up and an attempt will be made to
repass them, but Democratic leaders
have little hope that they can obtain
the necessary two-thirds vote.

Douglas. Ariz.. Feb. 4.-Agua Prieta,
the scene of one of the flercest battles
Of the Madero revolution was thrown
into panic to-day when bands of men
who declared they were Vasquistas from
Chihuahua suddenly appeared and began
raiding ranches near the border. Treas
ure vaults Of banks and stores were has
tiy emptied and the contents brought
into Douglas.


Refugees brought the report that the
bands were under Antonio Rodriguez. a
political prisoner liberated with thirty
others by sympathizers from the Jail at
Magdalena several days ago


One of the bands. comprising thirty
men, raided the Elias ranch. twelve
miles southwest of Douglas. last night.
Twelve American cowboys forced them
to retreat from the corrals and abandon
eighteen horses and saddles which they
had attempted to take The cowboys
opened fire on the raiders as they fed.
and they left behind one man seriously
wounded.

The old Japanese custom was to keep
all deaths of public personages concealed
from public knowledge. Even recently 1t
has been thought that the deaths Of
prominent men were not announced until
some days after they occurred.
So when reports of the critical illness
|of the emperor were given out some
weeks ago many people thought that he
were given out simply to prepare people
for the real news. But it soon became ap-
parent that a new policy was being fol-
lowed. the policy of taking the whole
emperor's condition. In fact. the bulletins
recorded symptoms and treatments that
would hardly be given to the public In
an American paper.


nation was watching at the bedside, and


we read that the emperor occupied a bed
three feet high in the center of apart
ments furnished otherwise in Japanese
style. The cars that skirt the palace
grounds went at slow speed all those days.
The fire gongs had been silenced, for he
was always SO concerned for his people


when the fire bells sounded. The tele-
phones were used instead for fire warn
ing.


Outside the moat, around the inner pal
ace grounds. is a large gravel plaza, and
here multitudes came to pray for the
life of their emperor Lines of school
girls bowling on the ground in the hot
sun, their teachers walking back and
forth tanning them: groups and scattered


ones, old and young men and women.
Buddhist priests. ShintO priests, Chris
tians, many who perhaps never in their
hearts prayed before. bowed deep in the
dust and offered their prayers.
Far into the night the scene was the
same. the police directing the people as
Ito where they might bow. One night a
photographer let off his fiashlight, and
the people were so enraged at the desecra-
ton that they attacked and killed him.

Now, they have returned, and they

but they are hoping for an even big
ger crop next year. or the year after.

with his umbrella

llu swept INTO the street. Durty ne
gro was standing in the gutter The

looked back Upon seeing Judge Broyles
and the haste he was making, the ne
gro let out a whoop and started up the
street himself He evidently was mis-
taken in the object Of the judges
chase. This and the memory of sew
eral unpublished peccadillos gave him
the legs of the wind--and once more
the lavender lid merrily rolled away.


There is no telling what would have
happened had not small newsboy
Joined the chase. His arms being lit
tie nearer the ground than the judges,
he was able by means of swift de-
tour and sudden dip to rescue the
hat just as it was going into the side
entrance of the Piedmont hotel The

unfaded

ing charges preferred against the judge

Hagerstown, Md, July 2s.-While driving
along the road near the foot of the noun
tain below Pen Mar Friday night James
Rock of Youngstown was attacked by an
angry bull; the animal charging at the
horse and striking 1t with great force.
Fortunately the bull had been dehorned
and the horse was not injured.


In an effort to evade the savage attacks
of the bull the horse finally broke the har-
ness and got away. Rock jumped from
the buggy to protect the horse. when the
bull charged him and he was knocked
between the buggy and one of the wheels,
where the bull kept him by repeated
charges. Rock shielded himself behind
the wheel and belabored the bull with the
butt-end Of a whip until the whip was
broken to pieces.


Rock. after some trouble. got an old pis-
toll from under the buggy seat and fired
three times at the bulls head. After the
third shot the weapon refused to work,
but the bull, badly wounded. gave up the
fight and ran away. The encounter lasted
twenty minutes and Rock was nearly ex-
hausted.

denied that she was jealous OF

Oregon line. While It was standing.
two men craWled into the mail car and

crew to realize what had happened. He
ran back to a saloon that stood near
the track at Delta and borrowed re-
volver. Then running along the train,
keeping well in the shadows, he saw
the robber in the engine cab and fired
The bandit fell to the ground dead. The
other robbers, hearing the shot jumped
from the mail car They carried the
registered mail with them.


News of the robbery was sent out
and the sheriff hastily formed a posse
and started in pursuit

try to make their way either northward

Quail hunting by motor car is the
latest novelty for sportsmen. and, judg-
ing from the enthusiastic reports from
Texas, this method of getting full bag
not only adds much to the comfort and
pleasure of the sport, but also has it's
practical values.


Recently Roy Munger of Dallas, Tex,
accompanied by friends, made a hunting
trip to west Texas, using his Cadillac
touring car not only to get to the hunt
ing grounds, but actually employing the
car in the field. Mr.. Munger and his
party made the trip in his car overland
to Big Springs and drove thence about
sixty miles north.


The Munger party bagged nearly as
much game as the law allows. Blue
quail were killed in large numbers and
the duck hunting near Gail. Tex, where
the nights were spent, was declared all a
hunter could wish for.

falls assault been made upon any one

LINCOLN, Neb., March 29-Convict
Charles Davis stabbed and almost in
stantly killed Convict John Strong at the
state penitentiary this morning while the
inmates of the prison were leaving the
breakfast table.


Strong was a negro. Davis is a half
breed. The latter was seated directly
behind the man he killed.


The gong had just sounded to clear
the convicts from the table when Davis.
leaning over the interposing table, seized
Strong by the head and plunged the
knife into his throat. drawing the blade,
which was of razor keenness, back to-
ward the ear. The wind pipe was sew
cred and the large arteries were cut


Lives Only Few Minutes.


Strong leaped from his seat onto the
table in front Of him, ran down it and
out of the door into the dollhouse. He
lived only few minutes. Guard Charles
Berry seized Davis, who still held the
knife. The rest OF the men filed out Of
the dining room in order.


Davis is said to have been frequently
threatened by Strong and claims that he
killed the negro to guard his own life.
Strong, who, with q brother, was sent to
prison for murder, serving a life sentence,
had frequently secreted a knife from the
guards and used 1t on fellow convicts
with whom he had grievance, never
occasioning any serious wounds, however.

From the Ohio State Journal.


No fairer sight these vernal days than
the big green trees and the west wind
playing together. They are as jolly COM
panions as a small boy and a Newfound-
land pup. and play very much alike. How
the wind seems to enjoy its wrestling and
tumblfng about with the big branches
and making the leaves wave their hands
and laugh. There is a hip, hip and hur-
dab. when the wind pitches in and bends
the limbs down until they CULVER with
delight.


And then. when the wind, tired for a
moment with the play. retires to get its
breath see the emerald branches resume
their composure. and standing erect. with
tranquil mien and joyful anticipation.
banter the west winds to come on again.
That defiance is beautifully tantalizing.
and soon the wind. gathering its airy
forces, about it. leaps from it's repose and
snatches the branches and hurls them
this way and that. and hugs and kisses
them in the very riot Of ecstasy until It
grows weary and retires to await another
banter. Didn't you ever see this lovely
sight? Well, look out where the trees
and blue skies meet. There's the play
ground.

Justice Ankeney gave him prelimi-
nary hearing and held him for the action

Among the Hop the women are far
from occupying the servile or subordinate
position. The women own the houses.
the wife receives the newly married hus-
band into her home: the children belong
to her clan and receive her clan name.
She is considered the owner of all house.
hold goods, food supplies and other pos
sessions of the family. The men perform
all outside and field labor. cut and carry
the wood for fuel, attend to the live
stock, and see that the wants of their
wives and children are provided for. In
civilized communities this would all be
considered matter Of course. but among
the American Indians ii is nowhere paral-
leIed This is by no means all that is
expected of the Hopi husband. They
must shear the sheep, card the wool and
weave blankets. belts, ceremonial robes
and even drsses and shawls for the wom-
en- On occasion they must even mind
the babies and help with the housework.
Strangely enough, the women build the
houses, although the men must cut the
timbers on distant mesas, transport them
to the villages on the back of mules or
burros, and place them in position as
ordered by the builders.

Washington. Aug 13.-By a process
of chicanery Speaker Clark effected to-
dsy the overruling of the Presidents
veto Of the wool bill. Fewer than two
thirds of the members recorded as pres
ent voted to reject the veto. With
,wenty-one Republican insurgents vot-
ing with the Democrats, the vote was
IA 10 50 to pass the bill over the veto.
Ten members voted present" and the
House supposed the effort TO override
was lost until Speaker Clark ruled that
,hsse ten should not be counted in the
total when the computation was made
for the two thirds majority. The
speaker then declared the veto over
ridden by five votes.


Speaker Clark held that the Consti-
tuition made no provision for the re-
cording Of present" votes and that the
requisite majority consisted of two
thirds of those voting for or against
The bill. The Democrats would have
lacked two votes of the required two
thirds and only the high handed ruling
Of the Democratic Speaker saved them
from more obvious defeat.


Representative Gardner appealed from
the decision of the chair on the con-
struction Of the constitutional provi-
sion. but later withdrew the appeal.
Representative Mann, the minority
leader. said he believed the ruling To
be fair. EX-Speaker Cannon dissented
from this view. holding that the two
thirds requirement applied to every
member present at the time of tho vot-
ing. Representative Fitzgerald,
Democrat, held similar views. but sub
sequently qualified his dissent


Announcement of the vote was de-
ayed for fully five minutes while the
Speaker read precedents and the con-
stitutional provision affecting the over
riding of a Presidential veto. When
he announced that a two-thirds ma
jority had voted to pass the wool bill
over the veto the Democrats pounded
their desks and gave loud cries of ex-

nouncement that four British regiments

that the actual mutineers had been
promised immunity If they would not
attempt any more mutiny.


Two hundred American troops COM
manded by Major Arrowsmith, arrived

the United States legation Several
companies from the Philippines will be
ordered here unless the authorities
soon show they are able to control

Mrs. Bischoff. who was sixty-three

MONTREAL, Aug. 13.-wireless sta
tions all along the Canadian coast to-
day were on the lookout for messages
from the Allan liner Corsican, Montreal
to Liverpool, which reported her bows
stove I'm by collision with an iceberg.


Captain Cooks wireless to the Allan
line offices said the damage to the
ships stem was above the waterline,
that there was no danger, and that he
was proceeding on his way. The Cor
sican left Montreal with twenty-five
first class. sixty-two second class and
200 third class passengers.


Despite the reassuring message from
Captain Cook, the Allan officials, re-
membering the long delay in receiving
news of the Titanic disaster and the
conflicting reports flashed from wireless
station to wireless station up and down
the coast, were anxious to hear more
from the Corsican and eagerly awaited
news


The first message from Captain Cook
said that the Corsican had struck a low
lying berg In latitude 52.24 north and
longitude 50. west. The steamer Lake
Champlain was the first to pick UP the
signal OF distress. and replied that she
was hurrying to the rescue.


Almost Immediately came other mes
sages from the Corsican, stating that
the damage was slight. The captain re-
ported that the injury to the vessel was
slight; that the Corsican would proceed
to Liverpool. That the liner was not
seriously damaged was attributed to
the fact that she was under reduced
speed.


The Allan Company today announced
that another wireless message was re-
ceived today from Captain Cook. con-
firming the first announcement that the
Corsican was not seriously damaged,
and giving more details Of the collision
with the iceberg. When the low berg
was sighted. said Captain Cooks mes
sage. the ships engines were reversed,
but not in time, and she touched the
iceberg. Her bow was slightly stove,
all damage being above the water line.


Captain Cook said he was proceeding
slowly toward Liverpool


BOSTON. Aug. 13.-General Manager
Bryce J. Allan, of the Allan line Of
fees here, today stated that although
the Canadian office had heard no fur
ther word from the liner Corsican, which
struck an iceberg off Belle Isle, near
Newfoundland, he felt certain that both
steamship and passengers were safe.


From the reports received OF the
accident" he said, II believe that the
rule Of this line to proceed with ex-
treme caution when in a fog or in the
vicinity OF icefields prevented another
horrible marine tragedy"

From Saratoga, where New York Republicans are
gathering for the State convention that will open
Wednesday, come curious reports about the party
sentiment.


Last April Barnes managed the Rochester con-
vention with ease and adopted a thoroughly reac.
tionary platform, which he sent Tory delegation
to the Chicago convention.


Following the nomination theft at Chicago, the
progressves left the party and formed Of their
own. II was thereupon supposed-indeed, il seemed
obvious-that the September convention would be
mere Formally; none but Tories would be left and
Barnes would have everything his own way.


But the Saratoga preliminares do not bear out
this forecast. Instead, it develops that many Re.
pubcans still remain in the party who want 1t to be
progressive; who insist that it shall get in line with
modern opinion who intend to make one more fight
{. inst the absolutism Of the Barnes-blackhorse
machine. These are appearing on the ground, to
voice their protest for the last time.


They represent the moderate supporters OF the
old Hughes regime; men who have been slow to be-
lieve the Republican party would surrender complete
ly to reactionary influences and who have not been
willing formally to withdraw from it until they have
made one more fight for better ideals.


This fight they will make in the convention this
week. Barnes has assured them that he will not try
to boss the convention; the old assurance that
BOSSES always give JUST as tney are getng reaoy to
boss. Barnes will.name the candidate and make the
platform; and when he has done it, this resduum of
moderately progressive Republicans still left inside
the party will realize, finally and decisivey, that
they have no place there.


The unseeing and unthinking extremists who
have undertaken to deliver the Republican party,
bound and gagged, into control Of reactionsm, are
simply putting on the second act. They drove out
the more vigorous and determined progressives by
their course at Rochester and Chicago now they are
driving out the moderates; and when the Saratoga
gathering has done its work. when Barnes shall have
declared against all primaries against all progressive
measures, against every instrumentalty of popular
rule, then the next division Of progressves will march
out Of the Republican party and there will be left
nothing but the husk Of the organization.


1t is not material whom Barnes may nominate
for governor He will not blind the State or country
to the fact that it is tool Of Barnes and the old
guard. The candidate plus the platform, plus the
demonstration Of Barnes complete control, will be
enough. The moderate progressives, the people who
recognize that this is the twentieth century, and who
do1't prefer the eighteenth, will be compelled to
break away from the party; and their exodus will
complete the assurance Of RooseveltStraus victory
this fall.

LONDON, March 25.-The twenty
fifth day of the national coal strike
ends with nearly 100000 workers idle,
many thousands dependent upon char
ity, every manufacturing industry
throttled and settlement remote.


The sanguine expectation at the be-
ginning of the day was that the joint
conference of coal owners and miners,
dramatically summoned by the premier,
would reach an agreement, but gloom
lest forebodings followed the news that
no joint coference was held.


For two and a half hours the prime
minister and his colleagues labored
with the coal owners, and for four
and half hours with the miners, but
they failed so completely that it was
deemed inadvisable to bring the dis
putants together again.


The government resorted to secrecy,
the only information being, THE con-
ference adjourned until tomorrow.
Everybody Silent


With everybody pledged to silence,
tomorrow events can not be forecast.
The one fact looms-government in
tervention has proved futile.


The main hope is that the miners
will break away from their leaders
and resume work. Their funds are
dwindling and the men may take this
step if the owners concede the princi-
pie of the minimum wage.


If a settlement is not reached by the
end of the week all passenger trains
on every branch line in the United
Kingdom may be suspended. The gem
eral managers met today and agreed
that this step would be necessary.


The working classes are undergoing
unspeakable suffering. No such situ-
alton in many years has faced the gov
ernment and the people. Measures
must be taken speedily to avoid disas-

NEW YORK, September 14.-Dan
Brogan. foreman of the gang working

feet below the street level when he
heard a scrambling noise and the
sound Of groans and curses coming
from the platform suspended below
him, where three men had been work
ing under his orders. He peered down,
but the lights carried by the three
workers had gone out. There was a
muffled cry for help.


Two Men Gripping the Edge.

pipe which runs the length of the
shaft, slid down to the lower platform,
and there, with the light of his own
lamp. saw that the thing had tipped
Two men were hanging to it, gripping
the edge with their hands. and unable
to hoist themselves till Brogan gave

and told him that Patrick O'DonnelI

darkness. where the water stood twen-

Brogan could hear splashing in the

The completion of the long-distance

mendabIe achievement


The laying of this underground cable
has been accomplished so quietly during
the past two years that it has occa-
stoned only casual mention. While

great engineering difficulties, the
achievement IS none the less notable
because of its cost and added efficiency

Hereafter communication will be open,
even under circumstances which have
formerly interrupted the telegraph.


The motive for building the under
ground conduit for telephone use was
better service The fact was cstab-
lishcd years ago that underground
wires afforded better facilities than
those overhead, and the growth of
the telephone service between Wash
ington and New York finally gave
warrant for the construction of a sub
way between the two points, connect
ing, Of course. with the large cities and
smaller towns along the route. Un-
dergrouud wires not only escape dis
placement by storms. but they arc free
from many weather disturbances which
make telephone communication difficult


The trunk line from Washington TO
New York is naturally only the begin
ming Of similar constructions in other
parts OF the country. In the nature
OF things. the line will in time be cx-
tended TO Boston, branch lines will be
built, and the underground service will
grow apacc. II will not be a cheaper
service. but it will be more satisfac-
tory and efficient, and in that lies the
certainty Of its extension.

quiet within the town. Not less than

warships Saturday.

Saturday was followed by an immediate
demand for the surrender or the de-
struefion of two Turkish torpedo boats
lying III the harbor.


The demand was refused promptly
and after short delay the Italians
opened fire, the shells causing great
damage. Three torpedoes finally de-
stroyed the Turkish vessels. The Turks
fought Bravely, but were at great
disadvantage. as they were unable to
maneuver their vessels, and their guns
were of small caiiber.


During the fighting in the harbor a
mob looted the government arsenal and
seized rifles and ammunition. One
shell burst close to an American build
ing, but injured no one All Ameri-
cans in the city are safe.

WASHINGTON, Oct 5.-That the
long expected battle between American
marines and Nicaraguan rebels was
fought yesterday at Barranca hill was
the information received at the state
department today in a cablegram from
Minister Wetzel at Managua


This stated that American marines
charged up Barranca hill and dislodged
the forces of General zeledon, the rebel
leader, which were intrenched at that
point.


The minister reported that several
American marines were killed and that
General Zeledon had been fatally
wounded. The battle lasted for 81
minutes and was fiercely fought.


An earlier dispatch received by Min
lister Castrilo, of Nicaragua, from the
minister of foreign affairs at Managua,
stated that four American marines had
been killed and six wounded in the
fighting.


Barranca hill is located near the
town of Coyotepa, which was afterward
occupied by the American forces


Rebels Ordered to Vacate.


Previous dispatches to the state de-
.partment said that the American COM
mander in Nicaragua Admiral South
erand, had given General Zeledon "a
hours notice to vacate Barranca hill
and allow the passage of the American
forces. The time limit of this ulti-
matum expired at 10 a IN. yesterday,
but nothing had been heard as to the
outcome until the receipt Of today's
dispatches.


later cablegram to the Nicaraguan
legation here says that 100 Nicaraguan
government troops were killed and 200
wounded.


General Ieledon was fatally wounded
and captured eight miles from Masaya
while retreating from Barranca hill
and died shortly afterWard.


Rapid Fire Guns Effective.


The use of rapid fire guns on both
sides of the hill is supposed to have
done fearful execution among the reb-
els at the top. According to the re-
ports received, the marines opened up
with their rapid fire guns for fifteen
minutes and during that time silenced
the fire of the rebels


Five hundred men were stationed on
one side and 400 opposite them. The
reports state that the marines soon got
the range of the intrenchments and
swept the hill with a terrific cross fire.
There was no opposition of serious
nature when the charge up the hill was
begun.

Efrem Zimbalist, the noted Russian

preciative audience yesterday afternoon
at the Columbia Theater.


The programme was varied, represent

tional Brahms sonata, through q stately
old dance with variations from Bach's
English suite. and finishing with a clus-
ter Of modern pieces by Scott, Zim-
balist. and Hubay-

depreciation which Brahm requires. The
long pedal point in the first movement Is
a remarkable feature Of this sonata.
Opus los" OF Brahms The adagio was
played with simplicity and without over
str aimed emotion. The third movement
has the conflicting rhythm Of which
Brahm makes such frequent use. 1t
was given with exquisite delcacy. The
last movement went with manly energy.

full sympathy with the sixteenth century

carefully and delightfully."- interpreted.

sian" are interesting for the embodiment

Cherry Ripe" dainty and bird-hke; tho
Irish Song" full Of pathetic Celtic mood.
and a Dance" by Cyril Scott. Were

Galveston. April 2L-The freight steam
er Elsud. Of the Southern Pacific Line,
and the passenger boat Denver. OF the
Mallory Line. crashed together in a
dense fog late last night, on the Calves
ton bar. Two lives were lost. those OF
deckhands who were knocked overheard
and one colored deckhand Of the Elsud
was badly hurt.


The crash occurred about fifteen miles
from the Bolivar light For a time II
was feared that the Elsud would sink.
The Elsud made for the shore. and was
beached on Galveston bar. She was
saved from sinking by her forward bulk
head having withstood the thrush of the
sea as the bow plates were ripped on.


There were about a hundred passengers
1on the Denver and a crew OF seventy.
There was a wild rush for life preservers
and the lifebOats OF the Denver after
the crash, but Capt. Charles p. Staples
and First Ohicer Lamb succeeded in
Quieting the excited passengers.


The dense fog alone is responsible for
the crash. The Denver was bound for
Galveston from New York. and had run
into the mist bank just after midnight.
The speed was reduced. and the vessel
vas making Ettle more than eight knots
an hour when the El Sud was struck


Look-outs Were Doubled.


The FL Sud. carrying a crew Of seventy,
was bound Ofor New York with a maxi
mum cargo. and was also under reduced
speed. Her commander. Capt. Forbes,
had doubled the look-outs. having men
in the bow as well as in the crows nest.
The two steamships came together with
a crash that hurled those on the Dem
ver's deck from their feet. while those
in the stateroOms were thrown out Of
their hunks. After the crash the vessels
sheered of.


All OF the passengers on board the
Denver were on deck, most Of them In
night attire. before the steamship had
stopped and were adjusting their life
belts.


Six OF the crew OF the El Sud were
standing at the port side Of the vessel,
well toward the bow. when the two
steamers came together. They were all
hurled across the deck. Three OF them
went overheard. Only one OF the men
could swim.

In Manitoba the Canadian government will sell
l72 grain elevators August 81 next, in which over
ST 100000 of the governments money has been
sunk, and which have been the constant center of
political intrigue and scandal for two years. The
investment was originally made upon the theory that
the government should enter into competition with
privately owned elevators, and thereby prevent the
exploitation of the agricultural communities. The
experiment proved failure. In the same province
four years ago all the telephone lines were pur-
chased by the government at high price, upon the
same theory; this ownership also proved f.ure


From Australia, also British territory, comes
the information that the only effective manner to
fl hit private monopoly is by government ownership
Of various interests-not merely telephone, railroad,
and street car systems, but coal mines and even
tenement houses. The report alleges that govern
ment ownership has -roved success there from
every viewpoint.


The failure in Manitoba and the success in Aus
tralia of government ownership proves that at the
bottom Of it all is the character of the people who
compose the government.

One Of the most remarkable achieve
ments OF the last few decades has been
the advance from the low, numbering
stage coach to the beautiful, swift-mov-
ing, luxurious motor car.


Yet some remarkable and very inter-
esting changes have taken place in the
construction of the car itself. The motor
car presents difficult but thoughtful
development along the lines of beauty,
elegance and efficiency.


Automobile building up to the present
time has been automobile experimenting.
Motor enthusiasts and the most scientific
engineers all over the world have been
searching by experiment and experience
for the principles of design and the par
ticular building materials that are the
essential factors in the safety of the car
that eventually will survive.


They have accomplished much, and the
present year gives motordom the very
highest type of automobile design and
construction.

CHICAGO, June 20.-With the asser-
ton that It's all over but the shout
ing" Congressman Mckinley. Taft's
campaign manager. gave out the fol-
lowing statement:


president Taft will be renominated
by the national Republican convention
now in session in Chicago.


Theodore Roosevelt has been elm
mated as a candidate before the con-
vention. Two test votes one Tues
day and another forced by his leaders
yesterday, have demonstrated that he
can not be nominated. The delegates
have repudiated his third term preten-
sions. His managers have resorted to
every known method of political STRAIT
egy, but without success. They have
attempted combinations with other
candidates, they have adroitly present
ed unfair and revolutionary plans of
procedure under the pretense of hon
esty and they have endeavored by
every means to make Taft delegates
break their solemn pledges and instruc-
tons In the face of these desperate
efforts, the Taft column has steadily
grown.


The Roosevelt followers, knowing
that their candidate can never get
enough votes to give him majority Of
the convention are now seeking in
hopeless and discouraged fashion for
another leader. Their search will be in
vain. President Taft's demonstrated
majority in the convention represents

ried away by a noisy. blustery. brag-

family.

ment In the stocks which the continent
threw over the previous week. but the
sharp rise in discount rates Tuesday, fore
casting a higher bank rate. weakened
home securities temporarily. The sign

isfactory arrangements of the Paris set

tions at the time. although dear money
following the annOuncement of the in
creased bank rate later checked specula-
tive ventures. Some big houses which

slump gradually sold stocks on each rise

weekend trading. while nervousness was
created by the spread of the Balkan con-
fiict. ConSols were exceptions to the gen.
eral tendency and quite firm. After
touching 12H they advanced and closed at
13 5-16. Mexican issues were weakened
by reports of another revolutionary
movement in Mexico.

The delegates from Nanking succeeded
in escaping yesterday from the burning
residences where they were the guests OF
the city. They are now staying at .
hotel in the legation quarter.


The streets have been thronged all
day. but all the shops and houses are
closed. Long lines or carts continue to
bring Saluables into the legation quar-
ter. where they are stored in foreign
banks and warehouses


In the legation quarter only few of
the better class Chinese are being per-
mitted to take refuge. Many Christians
are being taken care of in the mission
compounds. The trains departing for
Tientsin are crowded with refugees.


The number of killed during last nights
disturbances probably is under 100. The
object of the rioters evidently was loot
and not slaughter, and the continued
firing apparently was designed to frighten
the people.
